notes.title: Weight memory rule of thumb
notes.body: Weight memory = parameters x bytes per parameter. FP32 = 4 B, FP16/BF16 = 2 B, INT8 = 1 B, INT4 = 0.5 B. A 7B model in FP16 needs about 14 GB just for weights; add KV cache and runtime overhead for inference.

notes.title: Training compute rule of thumb
notes.body: Training FLOPs are approximately 6 x N x D, where N = parameters and D = training tokens. Chinchilla suggests about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training.

notes.title: Why decoding is memory-bound
notes.body: At small batch sizes each generated token needs all weights read from memory, but does little math per byte. Memory bandwidth (HBM), not peak FLOPs, usually limits tokens per second.

notes.title: Roofline model
notes.body: Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved. If it is above the hardware ratio (peak FLOPs / memory bandwidth) the work is compute-bound; below it, memory-bound. Large-batch training is usually compute-bound; small-batch decoding is memory-bound.

notes.title: Inference compute per token
notes.body: A forward pass costs about 2 x N FLOPs per token (N = parameters). Training costs about 6 x N per token because the backward pass is about twice the forward pass.

notes.title: KV cache size
notes.body: Per token, the KV cache stores a key and a value for every layer: about 2 x layers x (kv heads x head dim) x bytes per value. Multiply by context length and batch size. Grouped-query attention shrinks it by sharing KV heads.

notes.title: Workflows vs agents
notes.body: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization). Agents let the LLM dynamically direct its own steps and tool use. Start with the simplest option that works.

notes.title: PagedAttention and continuous batching
notes.body: vLLM stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like OS memory pages, which cuts fragmentation and allows more concurrent requests. Continuous batching adds new requests as soon as others finish instead of waiting for the whole batch.

notes.title: What context engineering is
notes.body: Context engineering is choosing everything that goes into the model's context at each step: system instructions, tool definitions, retrieved documents, memory and message history. Context is a finite budget, and quality drops as it fills (context rot), so aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens. Techniques: compaction (summarize history), structured note-taking outside the context, sub-agents with clean contexts, and just-in-time retrieval through tools.

notes.title: What an agent harness is
notes.body: The harness is the software around the model: it runs the agent loop (model -> tool call -> run tool -> feed result back), defines the tools, manages context and memory, enforces permissions and sandboxing, and decides when to stop. The same model can perform very differently in different harnesses. "Evaluation harness" means something else: a framework for running benchmarks against models, such as EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness.

notes.title: AI coding CLIs
notes.body: Terminal agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Aider) read and edit files, run commands and tests, and use git. They load project instructions from files such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, ask permission for risky actions, and can run non-interactively in scripts and CI (for example claude -p "prompt").

notes.title: MCP in one page
notes.body: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Roles: the HOST is the AI app (e.g. Claude Code, an IDE); inside it, a CLIENT keeps a 1:1 connection to each SERVER; a server exposes capabilities. Server primitives: TOOLS (functions the model can call), RESOURCES (data the app can read, like files or records) and PROMPTS (reusable templates). Clients can offer SAMPLING (a server asks the client's model for a completion) and ROOTS. Transports: stdio for local servers, Streamable HTTP for remote ones. Messages use JSON-RPC 2.0. Why it matters: write a tool once and use it in any MCP host, instead of a custom integration per app. Risks: untrusted servers, tool poisoning and prompt injection, so apply least privilege and require user approval for risky actions.

notes.title: Agent patterns
notes.body: An agent is an LLM that decides its own next steps and tool calls in a loop (ReAct: think, act, observe). Simpler WORKFLOWS follow fixed code paths. Common patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers (a lead model splits work and delegates), evaluator-optimizer (one model critiques, another improves), and multi-agent handoffs. Building blocks: tools, memory (short-term context plus long-term stores), planning, guardrails and tracing. Start with the simplest design that works; add autonomy only when it pays off. A2A is a protocol for agents to talk to other agents; MCP connects an agent to tools.

notes.title: How to evaluate an LLM app
notes.body: 1) Do error analysis: read many real outputs and list the failure modes. 2) Build a golden dataset of representative inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria. 3) Pick metrics per task: code-based checks (exact match, JSON schema, unit tests, regex) where possible; LLM-as-a-judge for open-ended quality; human review for the hardest cases. 4) Calibrate any LLM judge against human labels before trusting it, and watch for position, verbosity and self-preference bias. 5) For RAG, score retrieval (context precision/recall) and generation (faithfulness, answer relevance) separately. 6) Run offline evals in CI before every release, and online evals and monitoring on live traffic. Tools: promptfoo, DeepEval, Ragas, OpenAI Evals.

notes.title: Reading benchmarks wisely
notes.body: Model benchmarks: MMLU (knowledge, 57 subjects), GPQA (graduate-level, Google-proof science), HumanEval (code, pass@k), SWE-bench (fixing real GitHub issues), ARC-AGI (abstract reasoning), Humanity's Last Exam (frontier expert questions), LMArena (human preference votes, Elo-style ratings), HELM (many scenarios and metrics). Hardware benchmarks: MLPerf Training and Inference measure system speed on standard workloads. Pitfalls: contamination (test data leaked into training), saturation (top models all near 100%), prompt and setup differences between labs, and the gap between benchmark tasks and your real use case. Always confirm with your own evals on your own data.

notes.title: What a decision model is
notes.body: A decision model turns inputs (facts, predictions, preferences) into a choice. Main families: rules and decision tables (explicit logic), decision trees and ensembles (learned from data), decision theory (choose the action with the highest expected utility), sequential models such as MDPs and reinforcement learning (a policy picks actions over time), and multi-criteria methods (weigh several goals). Modern AI agents also make decisions, usually by an LLM choosing the next tool or step.

notes.title: Decision trees
notes.body: A tree asks yes/no questions about features and ends in a leaf with a class or value. Splits are chosen to make the groups purer, measured by Gini impurity or entropy (information gain) for classification and variance for regression. Easy to read and explain, but a single deep tree overfits; limit depth, require a minimum number of samples per leaf, or prune.

notes.title: Random forests and gradient boosting
notes.body: Ensembles combine many trees. A random forest (bagging) trains trees on random samples and random feature subsets, then votes or averages, which lowers variance. Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) adds trees one at a time, each fixing the errors of the previous ones. Boosted trees are still often the best choice for tabular business data.

notes.title: Decision theory and expected utility
notes.body: Rational choice under uncertainty: for each action, multiply each outcome's utility by its probability and add them up; pick the action with the highest expected utility. A decision tree in this sense (decision analysis) has decision nodes (squares), chance nodes (circles) and outcomes. An influence diagram is a compact graph of the same decisions, uncertainties and values. Expected value of information tells you how much a test or extra data is worth.

notes.title: Markov decision processes (MDPs)
notes.body: An MDP has states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor (gamma). The goal is a policy (state → action) that maximizes expected total discounted reward. Solve small MDPs with value iteration or policy iteration (Bellman equation). A POMDP adds hidden state: the agent only sees observations and keeps a belief. Reinforcement learning learns a good policy from experience when the transitions are unknown.

notes.title: Rules, decision tables and DMN
notes.body: Business decisions are often written as rules or decision tables: each row is a rule with input conditions and an output. A hit policy says what happens when several rows match (Unique, First, Priority, Collect...). DMN (Decision Model and Notation, from OMG) standardizes decision tables, decision requirement diagrams and the FEEL expression language, and is supported by engines such as Camunda, Drools and IBM ODM. Rules are transparent and auditable; ML models handle patterns too complex to write by hand. Many systems combine both: ML scores, rules decide.

notes.title: Multi-criteria decisions
notes.body: When a choice has several goals (cost, speed, quality, risk), multi-criteria decision analysis helps. Weighted scoring: give each criterion a weight, score each option, add weighted scores. AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) builds the weights from pairwise comparisons. Pareto-optimal options are those you cannot improve on one criterion without making another worse.

notes.title: From prediction to decision: thresholds and costs
notes.body: A classifier outputs a probability; the decision is where you set the threshold. Pick it from the costs of errors, not a default 0.5: if a missed fraud costs 50 times more than a false alarm, flag at a much lower probability. Use the confusion matrix, precision/recall and expected cost to choose. For high-stakes decisions, add human review for uncertain cases, log every decision with its reasons, and check for bias across groups.

notes.title: Liquid AI and Liquid Foundation Models (LFM)
notes.body: Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) are made by Liquid AI, a Boston-based AI company and spin-off from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), founded in 2023. The models were pioneered by MIT researchers Ramin Hasani, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini and Daniela Rus, and are designed as a non-Transformer, efficiency-focused alternative for both on-device and cloud deployment. It grew out of liquid neural networks: liquid time-constant networks whose neurons follow differential equations, inspired by the small nervous system of the C. elegans worm. Its Liquid Foundation Models are not plain Transformers. LFM1 (2024) came in 1B, 3B and 40B mixture-of-experts sizes. LFM2 (2025) is a hybrid of short convolution blocks and grouped-query attention, released with open weights in small sizes (about 350M to a few billion parameters) for fast, low-memory use on phones, laptops, cars and other edge devices; LFM2-VL adds vision. Later releases include LFM2.5 and LFM3, for example the LFM3-VL-2B vision-language model (see the LFM3-VL-2B benchmarks note). The LEAP platform helps developers run LFMs on device. You can try the models in the Liquid Playground (playground.liquid.ai) or read more on the official website (liquid.ai). AMD led its 2024 funding round. Why it matters: a strong alternative to Transformers when memory, speed and privacy on the device matter more than top benchmark scores.

notes.title: LFM3-VL-2B benchmarks vs other small vision-language models
notes.body: Vendor-reported averages across 10 categories: LFM3-VL-2B (1.9B params) 71.4; LFM2.5-VL-3B (3.1B) 57.6; MiniCPM-V 4.7 1B (1.6B) 57.5; Qwen 3.5 2B (2.3B) 64.0; Gemma 4 E2B (5.1B) 53.6; Gemma 4 12B 71.7; GPT-5.6 Luna 73.4; Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite 70.0. LFM3-VL-2B scores per category: General 66.0, Perception 75.6, Document/OCR/Chart 83.9, Math and logical reasoning 68.8, Visual grounding 77.3, Embodied reasoning 64.4, GUI understanding 83.1, Video 61.2, Multilingual 84.4, Agentic 42.5. Takeaways: a 1.9B model roughly matches Gemma 4 12B on average and beats every other small model in every category; it is strongest on documents, GUI and multilingual tasks; agentic tasks are its weak spot (42.5 vs 56.1 for GPT-5.6 Luna and 62.4 for Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite). These are the vendor's own numbers, so confirm on your own tasks.

notes.title: What an LLM engineer should know (checklist)
notes.body: 1) Model choice: capabilities, quality, license, open vs API. 2) Benchmarks and evals: public benchmarks plus your own task tests. 3) Performance: latency (TTFT, time per output token), throughput (tokens/s, requests/s) and concurrency. 4) Capabilities: text, vision, voice, video, tool calling, structured output, reasoning, languages, context window. 5) Hardware sizing: VRAM for weights + KV cache + overhead, RAM, GPU type and count. 6) Optimization: quantization, batching, caching, speculative decoding, smaller or distilled models. 7) Serving: vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, Ollama or llama.cpp locally. 8) Context engineering: prompts, RAG, chunking, memory, MCP and tools. 9) Adapting models: prompt first, then RAG, then fine-tuning (LoRA). 10) Cost: price per million input/output tokens or GPU-hours. 11) Safety: guardrails, prompt injection, privacy, PII. 12) Production: monitoring, tracing, logging, versioning, fallbacks and rate limits.

notes.title: Benchmarks vs your own evals
notes.body: Public benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SWE-bench, HumanEval, MMMU, LMArena Elo) give a first shortlist, but scores can be inflated by contamination (test data seen in training) and vendor-chosen settings. Always build a small eval set from your real tasks: inputs, expected outputs and a scoring method (exact match, rubric, LLM-as-a-judge checked against humans). Track quality together with latency and cost; the best model is the cheapest one that passes your bar.

notes.title: Latency metrics
notes.body: TTFT (time to first token): how long until the first word appears; driven by queueing and prefill (processing the prompt), so it grows with prompt length. TPOT / ITL (time per output token, inter-token latency): speed of decoding, usually memory-bandwidth bound. End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + TPOT × output tokens. Report p50 and p95/p99, not just averages. Chat users feel TTFT most; long answers depend on TPOT. Rough reading speed is about 5-10 tokens per second, so streaming faster than that feels instant.

notes.title: Throughput and concurrency
notes.body: Throughput is total output tokens per second (or requests per second) the server delivers across all users. Batching many requests together raises throughput but can raise each user's latency, so tune for a latency target (for example p95 TTFT under 1 s) and then maximize throughput. Continuous batching and PagedAttention (vLLM) keep the GPU busy. Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. Cost per token = GPU cost per hour / tokens per hour.

notes.title: Capabilities and modalities
notes.body: Check what the model can take in and put out: text, images (vision), audio/voice (speech-to-text, text-to-speech, real-time speech-to-speech), video understanding or generation, and files such as PDFs. Also check tool/function calling, JSON or structured output, reasoning/thinking modes, context window size, languages (for example Arabic quality), and knowledge cutoff. Voice agents need low end-to-end latency (under about 800 ms per turn); video uses many tokens per second of footage, so it costs more and fills the context fast.

notes.title: Memory sizing: VRAM, KV cache and RAM
notes.body: VRAM needed ≈ weights + KV cache + activations/overhead (add about 10-20%). Weights = parameters × bytes per parameter (FP16 2 B, FP8/INT8 1 B, INT4 0.5 B): a 70B model needs ~140 GB in FP16 or ~35-40 GB in 4-bit. KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes; it grows with context length × concurrent users, and can exceed the weights for long contexts. GQA, FP8 KV cache and PagedAttention reduce it. System RAM should usually be at least the model size for loading; with offloading (llama.cpp) part of the model runs from RAM, much slower. Training needs far more: roughly 16-20 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision, before activations.

notes.title: Making LLMs faster and cheaper
notes.body: Quantization (FP8, INT8, 4-bit AWQ/GPTQ/GGUF) cuts memory and often raises speed with small quality loss; test it on your evals. Prompt/prefix caching reuses work for repeated system prompts. Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose tokens the big model checks in one step. Use smaller or distilled models for easy steps and route hard ones to bigger models. Limit max output tokens, trim context, and batch offline jobs (batch APIs are often about 50% cheaper).

notes.title: What an AI engineer should know (checklist)
notes.body: An AI engineer builds and runs AI features in real products. Core areas: 1) Programming: Python, Git, testing, APIs (REST, JSON), async code, SQL. 2) Math basics: linear algebra (vectors, matrices), probability and statistics, gradients. 3) ML fundamentals: supervised vs unsupervised, train/validation/test split, overfitting, metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC). 4) Deep learning: neural networks, Transformers, embeddings; PyTorch. 5) LLMs: prompting, context engineering, RAG, vector databases, agents, tool calling, MCP, fine-tuning (LoRA). 6) Data: collection, cleaning, labeling, pipelines, data quality and privacy. 7) Evaluation: offline evals, A/B tests, LLM-as-a-judge, human review. 8) MLOps/LLMOps: experiment tracking, model registry, CI/CD, containers (Docker, Kubernetes), monitoring, drift. 9) Infrastructure: cloud AI platforms, GPUs, serving, latency, throughput, cost. 10) Responsible AI: bias, safety, security (prompt injection), privacy, regulation such as the EU AI Act. 11) Product sense: pick problems where AI adds value, measure business impact, communicate trade-offs.

notes.title: AI engineer vs ML engineer vs data scientist vs LLM engineer
notes.body: Data scientist: analyzes data, runs experiments and builds models to answer business questions. ML engineer: trains, deploys and scales ML models (pipelines, serving, MLOps). AI engineer: builds products on top of AI models, often foundation models through APIs or open weights; strong in software engineering, integration, evals and deployment. LLM engineer: an AI engineer focused on LLMs (prompting, RAG, agents, serving, latency, GPU sizing). Roles overlap a lot; titles differ by company.

notes.title: ML fundamentals every AI engineer needs
notes.body: Split data into train, validation and test sets and never tune on the test set. Overfitting = great on training data, poor on new data; fix with more data, regularization, simpler models or early stopping. Bias-variance trade-off: too simple underfits, too complex overfits. Pick metrics by cost of errors: precision when false alarms are costly, recall when misses are costly, F1 to balance, AUC for ranking. Watch data leakage: features that would not be known at prediction time. Baselines first: a simple model or rule shows whether a complex one is worth it.

notes.title: MLOps and LLMOps basics
notes.body: Version everything: code (Git), data, prompts and models (model registry). Track experiments (MLflow, Weights & Biases). Automate tests and deployment with CI/CD; package with Docker and run on Kubernetes or managed services. In production, monitor quality, latency, cost and errors; detect data drift (inputs change) and concept drift (the meaning of the target changes) and retrain or update prompts. For LLM apps, add tracing (LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry), prompt versioning, guardrails and regression evals before each release.

notes.title: Responsible and secure AI
notes.body: Check models for bias across groups, explain important decisions, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes cases. Protect privacy: minimize personal data, mask PII, respect data residency. Defend against prompt injection, data exfiltration through tools, jailbreaks and insecure output handling (see OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications). Follow regulation such as the EU AI Act (risk-based duties) and frameworks such as NIST AI RMF. Log decisions and keep model and data documentation (model cards, datasheets).

notes.title: Containers and containerization
notes.body: A container packages an app with everything it needs (code, runtime, libraries, settings) into an image that runs the same way on a laptop, a server or the cloud. Unlike a virtual machine, containers share the host operating system kernel, so they start in seconds and use less memory. Key terms: Dockerfile (recipe), image (built package), container (running image), registry (store for images such as Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR), Docker or Podman (build and run), Kubernetes or OpenShift (run many containers across many machines: scaling, restarts, rolling updates).

notes.title: Why AI and LLMs need containers
notes.body: 1) Dependency hell: AI stacks need exact matching versions of Python, PyTorch, CUDA, cuDNN and drivers; a container freezes a working set. 2) Reproducibility: the same image gives the same results in training, testing and production. 3) GPU access: the NVIDIA Container Toolkit lets containers use the host GPUs; NVIDIA NGC and NIM ship ready, optimized containers. 4) Ready-made serving images: vLLM, TGI, Triton and Ollama all run as containers with one command. 5) Scaling: Kubernetes schedules GPU containers, autoscales replicas with traffic and restarts failed ones. 6) Portability: move between clouds or on-premises without rebuilding. 7) Isolation and security: AI agents that run code should do it inside a sandboxed container. Tips: keep model weights outside the image (mount a volume or download at start) to keep images small, pin versions, and do not run as root.

notes.title: Quantization
notes.body: Quantization stores model weights (and sometimes activations and the KV cache) in fewer bits: FP32 (4 bytes) → FP16/BF16 (2) → FP8/INT8 (1) → INT4/FP4 (0.5). Benefits: less memory (a 70B model drops from ~140 GB in FP16 to ~35-40 GB in 4-bit), faster decoding because fewer bytes move from memory, cheaper hardware, and models that fit on laptops and phones. Cost: some quality loss, larger at 3 bits and below and on math, code and long-context tasks. Types: post-training quantization (PTQ, after training: GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, bitsandbytes) vs quantization-aware training (QAT, the model learns to cope with low precision). Formats: GGUF (llama.cpp, Ollama, with levels such as Q4_K_M and Q8_0), GPTQ and AWQ (GPU serving in vLLM/TGI), FP8 and NVFP4 (native on NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell). QLoRA fine-tunes LoRA adapters on top of a 4-bit base model to save memory. Always compare the quantized model with the original on your own evals.

notes.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark
notes.body: A desktop "AI supercomputer" the size of a small book, shipped in October 2025 (about $3,999 for the 4 TB Founders Edition). Inside is the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip: a 20-core Arm CPU and a Blackwell GPU with 5th-gen Tensor Cores, sharing 128 GB of unified LPDDR5X memory (about 273 GB/s). NVIDIA quotes up to 1 petaFLOP of FP4 AI compute (with sparsity). It runs DGX OS (Ubuntu) with the full NVIDIA AI software stack (CUDA, NIM, NeMo), so code moves easily to DGX servers and the cloud. Use it to prototype, fine-tune and run models locally: inference on models up to about 200B parameters (in FP4) and fine-tuning up to about 70B. A built-in ConnectX-7 200 Gb/s network port links two Sparks to run models up to about 405B parameters. Partner versions with the same GB10 chip: ASUS Ascent GX10, Dell Pro Max with GB10, HP ZGX Nano, Lenovo ThinkStation PGX, MSI EdgeXpert, Acer Veriton GN100 and Gigabyte AI TOP ATOM.

notes.title: DGX Spark vs similar local AI machines
notes.body: NVIDIA DGX Station: the big brother, a deskside workstation with the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra chip and about 784 GB of coherent memory for much larger models. Apple Mac Studio (M3 Ultra): up to 512 GB unified memory with about 819 GB/s bandwidth, so very large models fit and generate tokens fast, but no CUDA (use MLX or llama.cpp). AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 ("Strix Halo") mini PCs such as the Framework Desktop or HP Z2 Mini G1a: up to 128 GB unified memory at about 256 GB/s, lower price, ROCm/Vulkan instead of CUDA. Consumer GPU PC with an RTX 5090: only 32 GB VRAM but about 1.8 TB/s, so much faster on models that fit. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell: 96 GB VRAM workstation card. NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor: a 128 GB module for robots and edge devices, not a desktop. How to choose: memory size decides which models fit; memory bandwidth decides tokens per second; software (CUDA vs MLX vs ROCm) decides what runs easily.

notes.title: Unified memory and the bandwidth rule
notes.body: In unified-memory machines (DGX Spark, Apple silicon, AMD Strix Halo) the CPU and GPU share one large pool, so models much bigger than a gaming GPU's VRAM can load. But decoding reads all active weights for each token, so a rough upper bound is tokens/s ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes of active weights. Example: a 70B model in 4-bit is about 35-40 GB; on DGX Spark (~273 GB/s) that gives under about 7 tokens/s, while a Mac Studio M3 Ultra (~819 GB/s) can roughly triple that. Mixture-of-experts models only read their active experts per token, so they run much faster on these machines. Spark is strongest at prefill (prompt processing), fine-tuning and FP4 compute thanks to its Blackwell Tensor Cores.

notes.title: GTA 6 and Rockstar's RAGE engine
notes.body: Grand Theft Auto VI was released in November 2026 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar Games built it on its own in-house engine, RAGE (Rockstar Advanced Game Engine), instead of a licensed engine such as Unreal Engine that many other studios use. RAGE has powered Rockstar games since 2006, including GTA IV, Red Dead Redemption, GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2, and it is written in C++ for speed and direct control of memory and hardware. What RAGE does: rendering (graphics, lighting), physics and animation (with Euphoria for realistic character movement), AI and simulation of the city (traffic, pedestrians, weather, day-night cycle), audio, scripting of missions, networking for online play, and streaming of the open world. Memory is the first problem: a PS5 has only 16 GB of shared GDDR6 memory (not 16 MB) for the whole game, far less than the size of the world. Three key techniques: 1) Streaming: load only what is near the player from the fast SSD and unload what is far away, so a huge map fits in limited memory. 2) Simulation: thousands of NPCs, cars and systems run with their own behavior, with less detail for things far from the player (level of detail). 3) Ray tracing: light, shadows and reflections calculated by following light rays for realistic images, using the console GPU's ray-tracing hardware. Link to AI: the same limits drive LLM engineering. Memory decides what fits, so engines stream and compress data just as LLM systems quantize models, manage the KV cache and offload weights, and both use C++ and GPU-specific code where speed matters.

notes.title: Physics problems in AI video generation
notes.body: Video models such as Sora, Veo, Kling, Runway and Seedance make very realistic clips, but they often break the laws of physics. Common failures: 1) Object permanence: things vanish, appear or merge when hidden behind something. 2) Gravity and motion: objects float, fall at the wrong speed or move in reverse. 3) Collisions: bodies pass through each other, glass does not shatter properly. 4) Cause and effect: a bitten cookie shows no bite mark, a ball changes direction for no reason. 5) Conservation: liquids appear or disappear, the amount of food changes. 6) Bodies and hands: extra fingers, limbs that bend the wrong way, faces that morph. 7) Consistency over time: clothes, text and backgrounds change between frames; longer clips drift more. Why it happens: the model learns how pixels usually look and move from training videos, not the rules behind them. It has no built-in 3D world, mass or forces, and rare events (breaking, splashing, complex collisions) are thin in the data. Research found models mostly imitate the closest training example ("case-based" generalization) and fail on new situations, even when made bigger. How it is measured: physics benchmarks such as VideoPhy, PhyGenBench and Physics-IQ, plus human review. How labs improve it: more and better-labeled video, synthetic data from physics simulators and game engines, 3D-aware "world models" (for example NVIDIA Cosmos and Google DeepMind Genie), training rewards for physical correctness, and longer context for consistency. Practical tips: keep shots short, avoid complex interactions (pouring, breaking, crowds of hands), use image-to-video with a good first frame, generate several takes and pick the best, and edit or composite the hard parts. Why it matters: realistic-looking but wrong physics is a problem for robotics and self-driving training, science and education, and it is also a clue for spotting AI-made videos.

notes.title: Z.ai (Zhipu AI) and the GLM models
notes.body: Z.ai is the international brand (since 2025) of Zhipu AI, a Beijing AI company spun out of Tsinghua University in 2019 and one of China's leading LLM labs. Its model family is GLM (General Language Model), named after the GLM pre-training method from Tsinghua research. Timeline: GLM-130B (2022, open bilingual Chinese-English model); ChatGLM-6B (2023, small open chat model that ran on consumer GPUs and became very popular); GLM-4 (2024); GLM-4.5 and GLM-4.5-Air (2025, mixture-of-experts: about 355B total / 32B active and 106B / 12B active parameters) built for reasoning, coding and agents, with a "thinking" mode; GLM-4.6 (2025) with a longer context window (about 200K tokens) and stronger coding. Later versions continue the line. Other models: GLM-4.5V / GLM-4.xV (vision-language), CogView (images) and CogVideoX (video). Many GLM models are released with open weights under permissive licenses (for example MIT), so you can download them from Hugging Face and run them with vLLM or SGLang. You can also use them through the Z.ai chat app and API, which is OpenAI-compatible, and a low-cost "GLM Coding Plan" that plugs into coding agents such as Claude Code, Cline and others. Why it matters: GLM models are among the strongest open-weight models for coding and agent tasks at a low price, alongside Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi. Things to consider: the US placed Zhipu on its Entity List in January 2025, so check compliance, data residency and your company's policy before using its hosted API; self-hosting the open weights avoids sending data to the provider.

notes.title: What are the weights of an LLM?
notes.body: Weights are the numbers a neural network learns during training. Each weight says how strongly one input or neuron affects the next one; together with small offsets called biases they are the model's parameters. "7B" or "70B" in a model name is the number of parameters: 7 or 70 billion learned numbers. Simple picture: a neuron multiplies each input by its weight, adds them up plus a bias, and passes the result through an activation function; an LLM is billions of these operations organized as large matrices. The weights hold everything the model "knows" (language, facts, skills), but spread across all the numbers, not stored as readable sentences, so you cannot point to the one weight that knows Paris is in France. The code of a model is small; the weights are what make it smart, which is why they are the valuable part companies keep closed or release as open weights.

notes.title: How weights are learned and used
notes.body: Training: weights start as random numbers. The model predicts the next token, a loss function measures the error, backpropagation computes how each weight contributed (the gradient), and an optimizer such as Adam nudges every weight a little to reduce the error. Repeating this over trillions of tokens is pre-training; it is the expensive part (thousands of GPUs, weeks to months). Inference: the weights are frozen; the model only reads them to turn your prompt into an answer, which is why inference is far cheaper than training. Fine-tuning continues training on new data to adjust the weights; LoRA freezes the original weights and trains small extra matrices instead, so it needs much less memory and the adapter is only a few megabytes.

notes.title: Where the weights live in a Transformer
notes.body: Embedding matrix: one vector of weights per token in the vocabulary. Attention layers: weight matrices that make queries, keys and values (Q, K, V) and an output projection (O). Feed-forward (MLP) layers: usually the largest share of the weights, often seen as where much factual knowledge is stored. Layer normalization: small scale and shift weights. Output head: turns the final vector into a score for every token. In mixture-of-experts models only some experts' weights are used per token: "active" parameters (for example 32B) vs "total" parameters (for example 355B). Weights are stored in files such as safetensors (Hugging Face) or GGUF (llama.cpp, Ollama), often split into shards. Do not confuse them with: activations (temporary values computed for each input), the KV cache (stored attention keys and values for the current context), and hyperparameters (settings chosen by people, such as learning rate or number of layers).

notes.title: Fine-tuning LLMs: what it is and when to use it
notes.body: Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own smaller dataset so its weights adapt to a task, style or domain. Try the cheaper options first, in this order: 1) prompt engineering and examples in the prompt, 2) RAG to give the model your knowledge, 3) fine-tuning. Fine-tune to change behavior: a fixed output format or tone, a narrow task done reliably (classification, extraction, tool calling), domain language (legal, medical, Arabic dialects), or to make a small cheap model match a big one on your task (distillation). Do not fine-tune mainly to add facts that change often: RAG is better for knowledge, because it is easy to update and can cite sources. Rule of thumb: RAG for what the model should know, fine-tuning for how it should behave.

notes.title: Types of fine-tuning
notes.body: Continued pre-training: more next-token training on large raw domain text (for example medical papers) to learn the domain language. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning: train on prompt → ideal answer pairs; this is how base models become chat assistants. Preference tuning: teach the model which of two answers people prefer. RLHF trains a reward model from human rankings then optimizes with reinforcement learning (PPO); DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) uses the preferred/rejected pairs directly and is simpler and cheaper. Reinforcement fine-tuning with verifiable rewards (for example GRPO, used for DeepSeek-R1 style reasoning): the model is rewarded when its answer can be checked as correct, such as math results or passing code tests. Distillation: train a small student model on the outputs of a large teacher model.

notes.title: Full fine-tuning vs LoRA and QLoRA
notes.body: Full fine-tuning updates every weight: best possible fit but very costly in memory (roughly 16-20 bytes per parameter with Adam, so a 7B model needs over 100 GB of GPU memory) and you store a full copy of the model for each task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) trains a tiny fraction of parameters. LoRA freezes the original weights and adds small low-rank matrices (rank r, for example 8-64) to attention and feed-forward layers; only those are trained, often under 1% of the parameters, and the adapter file is a few megabytes that can be swapped or merged into the model. QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters on top, so a 7-8B model can be fine-tuned on a single consumer GPU and a 70B model on one large GPU. Quality of LoRA is usually close to full fine-tuning for most tasks.

notes.title: Fine-tuning data, process and tools
notes.body: Data matters most: a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality, diverse, correctly formatted examples often beat a huge noisy set. Use the model's chat template (system, user, assistant turns), remove duplicates and personal data, and keep a separate test set the model never trains on. Process: 1) define the task and a success metric, 2) build a baseline with prompting or RAG, 3) prepare data, 4) pick a base model (size, license, language), 5) train (key settings: learning rate, epochs (often 1-3), LoRA rank, batch size), 6) evaluate against the baseline on your test set plus general and safety checks, 7) deploy (merge the adapter or serve it with vLLM multi-LoRA) and monitor. Tools: Hugging Face TRL and PEFT, Unsloth (fast, low-memory), Axolotl, torchtune, LLaMA-Factory; managed services: OpenAI fine-tuning API, Google Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker, Azure AI Foundry, Together AI. Pitfalls: overfitting (great on training data, worse on new data), catastrophic forgetting (the model loses general skills), weaker safety behavior after tuning, data leakage into the test set, and license limits on the base model or on using another model's outputs for training.

notes.title: CoWoS: how AI chips are packaged
notes.body: CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) is TSMC's advanced 2.5D packaging technology. Instead of putting one chip alone on a package, several dies (a big GPU or accelerator die plus stacks of HBM memory) sit side by side on a silicon interposer, a thin slice of silicon with very dense wiring. The interposer then sits on an organic package substrate that connects to the circuit board. Name breakdown: Chip-on-Wafer = the dies are bonded onto the interposer wafer; on-Substrate = that assembly is mounted on the substrate. Why AI needs it: an LLM accelerator is limited by memory bandwidth, and HBM only delivers terabytes per second when it sits millimetres from the GPU with thousands of short connections. Ordinary PCB wiring cannot do that. NVIDIA (A100, H100, H200, Blackwell B200/GB200), AMD Instinct (MI300X), Google TPUs and AWS Trainium all rely on CoWoS or similar packaging.

notes.title: CoWoS variants and the reticle limit
notes.body: A single chip cannot be bigger than the lithography "reticle" (about 858 mm²). CoWoS gets around this by joining several dies on an interposer that is several times the reticle size. Variants: CoWoS-S uses one large silicon interposer (H100: one GPU die + 6 HBM stacks). CoWoS-R uses an organic redistribution-layer (RDL) interposer, cheaper and more flexible. CoWoS-L uses an organic interposer with small embedded silicon bridges (LSI) only where dense links are needed, allowing even larger packages; NVIDIA Blackwell B200 uses CoWoS-L to join two reticle-size GPU dies with a 10 TB/s link plus 8 HBM3E stacks. TSMC plans ever larger interposers (several reticles) for future chips such as NVIDIA Rubin. Related: SoIC is TSMC's 3D stacking (dies on top of each other); competitors include Intel EMIB and Foveros, and Samsung I-Cube.

notes.title: CoWoS as the AI supply bottleneck
notes.body: From 2023 the shortage of AI GPUs was driven less by making the GPU dies and more by CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM supply. TSMC has been roughly doubling CoWoS capacity each year (by most estimates from about 15,000 wafers per month in 2023 to well over 60,000 by 2025-2026), and NVIDIA books the largest share. Outsourced packaging firms (OSATs) such as ASE/SPIL and Amkor add capacity, and TSMC is building CoWoS lines in Taiwan and planning packaging in Arizona. HBM comes from SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. Lesson for AI engineers: compute supply depends on the whole chain (wafer, HBM, packaging, power), and packaging is now a key strategic step, not an afterthought.

notes.title: ASML EUV lithography: the machines that print AI chips
notes.body: ASML (Veldhoven, Netherlands) is the only company in the world that makes EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines, which print the smallest features on leading-edge chips such as NVIDIA, AMD and Apple processors made by TSMC, Samsung and Intel. EUV uses light with a 13.5 nm wavelength, made by hitting tiny droplets of molten tin with a powerful CO2 laser about 50,000 times a second to create a plasma. Because EUV is absorbed by air and glass, everything happens in a vacuum and the light is steered by ultra-flat multilayer mirrors from Zeiss instead of lenses. Standard EUV machines (the NXE series, such as NXE:3800E) have a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.33 and cost about $150-200 million each. Export controls stop ASML from selling EUV machines to China, which makes EUV a key part of the AI chip race.

notes.title: High-NA EUV (ASML EXE series)
notes.body: High-NA EUV is ASML's next generation: the EXE:5000 and EXE:5200 machines raise the numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55. A higher NA lets the optics capture more angles of light, so the machine can print finer lines (resolution about 8 nm versus about 13 nm), roughly 1.7x smaller features and almost 3x the transistor density per exposure. This can replace multi-patterning (exposing the same layer several times), which saves steps and errors. Trade-offs: each machine costs about $350-400 million, is the size of a double-decker bus and weighs about 150 tonnes; it uses anamorphic optics, so the exposure field is half the size of standard EUV, which matters for very large AI chips that must be stitched. Intel was first to buy and install High-NA (for its 14A node); TSMC and Samsung are evaluating it for later nodes around 2027-2030. The next idea after this is Hyper-NA (NA about 0.75).

notes.title: Why lithography matters for AI
notes.body: Each new process node (for example TSMC N3, N2, A16) packs more transistors into the same area, giving AI accelerators more compute and better energy efficiency per watt, which lowers the cost of training and inference. EUV, and later High-NA EUV, is what makes those nodes possible. The AI chip supply chain therefore runs: ASML lithography machines → foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) making the dies → HBM memory (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron) → advanced packaging such as CoWoS → servers and data centres. A bottleneck at any step, including the small number of EUV machines ASML can build each year, limits how many AI chips the world can make.

notes.title: CUDA: NVIDIA's software moat
notes.body: CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture), launched by NVIDIA in 2006-2007, is a platform and programming model for running general-purpose code on NVIDIA GPUs. Developers write "kernels" (functions that run on thousands of GPU threads at once) in C/C++ or Python. On top sit libraries that AI depends on: cuBLAS (matrix maths), cuDNN (neural-network layers), NCCL (communication between GPUs), TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM (fast inference), plus CUTLASS for custom kernels. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, vLLM and most AI tools call these under the hood. Why it matters: almost two decades of tools, libraries, tutorials and trained developers make CUDA the default for AI, which is NVIDIA's biggest advantage ("moat") beyond the chips themselves. CUDA only runs on NVIDIA hardware. Alternatives: AMD ROCm/HIP, Intel oneAPI/SYCL, Apple Metal/MLX, and portable layers such as OpenAI Triton, OpenCL and Vulkan compute.

notes.title: AMD in AI
notes.body: AMD (Advanced Micro Devices, Santa Clara, CEO Lisa Su) is NVIDIA's main GPU competitor and also makes CPUs (Ryzen, EPYC). AI data-centre GPUs: the Instinct line, such as MI300X (192 GB HBM3), MI325X (256 GB HBM3E), MI350/MI355X (288 GB HBM3E, CDNA 4) and the MI400 series with Helios rack systems. Large memory per GPU is AMD's selling point: big models fit on fewer GPUs. Software: ROCm is AMD's open-source answer to CUDA, and HIP lets CUDA code be ported with small changes; PyTorch, vLLM and SGLang support ROCm, though CUDA still has the wider ecosystem. AMD bought Xilinx (FPGAs) and ZT Systems (rack-scale servers). Customers include Microsoft, Meta, Oracle and OpenAI. Consumer side: Ryzen AI chips with NPUs, Ryzen AI Max+ ("Strix Halo") with up to 128 GB unified memory, and Radeon gaming GPUs. Like NVIDIA, AMD is "fabless": TSMC manufactures its chips.

notes.title: Fabs, foundries and fabless chip companies
notes.body: A fab (fabrication plant) is a factory that makes chips on silicon wafers in an ultra-clean room, using hundreds of steps: deposition, lithography (EUV machines from ASML), etching, doping and polishing. A leading-edge fab costs $20 billion or more. Business models: Fabless companies design chips but do not own fabs (NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, Broadcom). Foundries make chips designed by others (TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, GlobalFoundries, SMIC). IDMs (integrated device manufacturers) design and make their own chips (Intel, Samsung memory, Micron, SK hynix). Process nodes such as 5 nm, 3 nm, 2 nm or A16 are now marketing names for each generation, not real measurements; smaller nodes give more transistors, speed and efficiency. Yield is the share of good chips per wafer and matters most for huge AI dies. Governments fund new fabs (US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act) because chips are strategic, and most leading-edge capacity is in Taiwan.

notes.title: TSMC: the foundry behind AI chips
notes.body: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), founded in 1987 by Morris Chang in Hsinchu, Taiwan, is the world's largest contract chip maker (foundry) with roughly two-thirds of the foundry market and most of the leading-edge share. It makes chips for NVIDIA (H100, Blackwell, Rubin), AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, Broadcom, Google TPUs, AWS Trainium and many others. It never sells chips under its own brand, so customers trust it with their designs. Process nodes: N5 and N4 (H100 is on a custom 4N), N3 (3 nm), N2 (2 nm, using gate-all-around nanosheet transistors, volume production from late 2025) and A16 (with backside power delivery). It also leads advanced packaging (CoWoS, SoIC), which AI GPUs need. TSMC is building fabs in Arizona (USA), Kumamoto (Japan) and Dresden (Germany). Risk: so much AI chip production in Taiwan creates geopolitical risk for the whole AI industry.

notes.title: Eval metrics: which score for which task
notes.body: Pick the metric from the task. Exact match and accuracy: for classification, multiple choice and short factual answers. Code: run unit tests; pass@k is the chance that at least one of k generated samples passes. Structured output: JSON schema validity, field-level accuracy. Text overlap metrics (BLEU for translation, ROUGE for summaries) compare words with a reference answer; cheap but they miss meaning and punish good paraphrases. Embedding similarity (BERTScore, cosine similarity) compares meaning instead of words. Open-ended answers (helpfulness, tone, correctness against a rubric): LLM-as-a-judge or human review. RAG: faithfulness (answer supported by retrieved context), answer relevance, context precision and context recall. Operational metrics belong in every eval too: latency, cost per request, token usage and refusal rate. Rule of thumb: use the cheapest deterministic check that captures the requirement, and save judges and humans for what code cannot check.

notes.title: LLM-as-a-judge: doing it well
notes.body: An LLM judge grades another model's output against a rubric. Good practice: 1) Give a clear rubric with concrete pass/fail criteria or a small scale (1-5) with examples for each score. 2) Prefer binary or pairwise judgments over fine-grained scores; they agree better with humans. 3) Ask for a short reasoning before the verdict, and return structured output (JSON). 4) Grade one criterion per call (for example correctness separately from tone). 5) Calibrate: label a sample by hand and measure agreement (accuracy, Cohen's kappa) between judge and humans before trusting it; re-check when the judge model changes. Known biases: position bias (prefers the first answer in pairwise; fix by swapping order), verbosity bias (prefers longer answers), self-preference (prefers its own model family) and leniency. Use a strong model as judge and keep the judge prompt under version control like any other code.

notes.title: Evaluating agents
notes.body: Agents take many steps, so evaluate both the result and the path. Outcome metrics: task success rate (did it finish the goal?), measured by checking the final state (tests pass, ticket closed, database row correct). Trajectory metrics: right tools chosen, correct tool arguments, number of steps, loops or repeated calls, recovery after errors. Efficiency: tokens, cost, wall-clock time per task. Safety: did it take forbidden actions, leak data or follow injected instructions? Because agents are non-deterministic, run each task several times and report pass rate (pass^k is the chance that all k runs succeed, a reliability measure). Public agent benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (fix real GitHub issues), Terminal-Bench (command-line tasks), tau-bench (customer-service tools with simulated users), WebArena and OSWorld (web and desktop use), GAIA (general assistant tasks). Build your own task suite from real user requests as soon as possible.

notes.title: Eval tooling and statistics
notes.body: Tools: promptfoo (CLI, config-based tests and red teaming), DeepEval (pytest-style LLM tests), Ragas (RAG metrics), OpenAI Evals, UK AISI Inspect (agent and safety evals), LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix and Langfuse (tracing plus datasets and online scoring). Run evals in CI so every prompt or model change is tested before release. Statistics matter: with 50 test cases, a change from 80% to 84% is usually noise; report confidence intervals (bootstrap) and use paired comparisons on the same cases. Grow the dataset from production failures. Watch for data contamination (benchmark questions leaked into training data) and for overfitting your prompt to a small eval set; keep a held-out set. Online evals: sample live traffic, score it with judges or user feedback (thumbs up/down, edits, retries) and track drift over time.

notes.title: Evaluating classifiers that drive decisions
notes.body: A confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the cases flagged, how many were right. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the real cases, how many were caught. F1 is their harmonic mean. Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data (with 1% fraud, always saying "no fraud" is 99% accurate). ROC-AUC measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds; PR-AUC is more informative when positives are rare. Calibration checks that predicted probabilities match reality (of cases scored 0.8, about 80% should be positive); check with a reliability diagram and fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression. Calibrated probabilities are needed for expected-cost decisions. Finally, translate errors into money: cost of a false positive versus a false negative, and pick the threshold that minimises total expected cost.

notes.title: Decisions under uncertainty: criteria and value of information
notes.body: When probabilities are known, choose by expected value or expected utility (utility captures risk aversion: losing $1M hurts more than winning $1M helps). When probabilities are unknown: maximin picks the action with the best worst case (cautious), maximax the best best case (optimistic), minimax regret minimises the largest "I wish I had chosen differently" loss, and the Hurwicz criterion mixes best and worst cases. A decision tree diagram (decision nodes as squares, chance nodes as circles) is solved by "rolling back": compute expected values from the leaves towards the root. Value of information: the expected value of perfect information (EVPI) = expected value with perfect knowledge minus the best expected value now; it is the most you should pay for a test, survey or extra data. Sensitivity analysis shows which inputs could change the decision.

notes.title: Bandits, experiments and sequential decisions
notes.body: A/B testing splits traffic evenly between options and decides at the end; simple and statistically clean, but it keeps sending users to the worse option during the test. Multi-armed bandits balance exploration (trying options to learn) and exploitation (using the best option so far) while learning. Common algorithms: epsilon-greedy (explore at random with probability epsilon), UCB (upper confidence bound: pick the option with the highest optimistic estimate) and Thompson sampling (sample from each option's posterior and pick the best sample). Contextual bandits use features of the user or situation, as in recommendations and ad selection. Full reinforcement learning (MDPs) is needed when actions change future states. In LLM systems, these ideas appear in model routing (choose a cheap or strong model per request), prompt selection, and RLHF, where a policy learns from rewards.

notes.title: LLMs and decision-making
notes.body: LLMs are increasingly used inside decisions: classifying tickets, approving refunds, routing requests, ranking candidates or choosing an agent's next action. Good design: let the LLM extract facts and give reasons, but keep hard rules and limits (amounts, eligibility, compliance) in deterministic code or DMN tables; ask for structured output with a decision and a confidence; route low-confidence or high-impact cases to a human (human-in-the-loop); log inputs, outputs and the model version for audit. Risks: inconsistent answers to the same input (use temperature 0, fixed prompts, several samples or majority vote), sensitivity to wording and order, hidden bias, and prompt injection in user-provided text. Evaluate the decision itself, not only the text: measure accuracy against labelled past decisions, cost of errors, fairness across groups and agreement with human experts.

notes.title: What an AI strategy is
notes.body: An AI strategy is a company's plan for using AI to reach its business goals: where AI will create value, what it will build, buy or partner for, which data, people, platforms and governance it needs, how it will manage risk, and how it will measure results. It is a business strategy first, not a technology shopping list. A good AI strategy answers: 1) Ambition: what business outcomes (revenue, cost, risk, customer experience) and by when? 2) Portfolio: which use cases, in what order? 3) Foundations: data, platforms, models and security. 4) Operating model: who owns AI, who builds, how decisions are made. 5) People: skills, AI literacy and change management. 6) Governance and responsible AI: policies, risk tiers, regulation. 7) Value tracking: baselines, KPIs and ROI. Common mistakes: starting from a tool instead of a problem, running many disconnected pilots ("pilot purgatory"), ignoring data readiness, and treating adoption as an afterthought.

notes.title: Why most AI pilots fail to scale
notes.body: Research in 2025 showed a big gap between AI experiments and results. Press coverage of MIT NANDA's report "The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025" said about 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots stall and deliver no measurable P&L return, while about 5% create large value. The study (about 150 leader interviews, a 350-employee survey and 300 public deployments) blamed a "learning gap": most tools do not retain feedback, adapt to context or improve over time, and are not integrated into workflows. It also reported that buying from specialised vendors and partnering succeeded about two-thirds of the time, versus about one-third for internal builds, and that budgets favour sales and marketing although the biggest returns were in back-office automation. Gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of rising costs, unclear value or weak risk controls, and warned about "agent washing". Lesson: pick problems with clear value, integrate deeply, and plan for adoption and scaling from day one.

notes.title: What AI high performers do differently
notes.body: McKinsey's State of AI survey (2025, repeated in 2026) defines AI high performers as the roughly 6% of organisations that attribute at least 5% of EBIT to AI and report significant value. Compared with others, they: 1) Fundamentally redesign workflows around AI instead of adding AI to old processes; workflow redesign was one of the strongest drivers of impact (about three times as likely). 2) Have senior leaders who visibly own and champion AI (about three times as likely). 3) Set growth and innovation goals, not only cost cutting. 4) Define when model outputs need human validation (human-in-the-loop). 5) Track KPIs and measure impact. 6) Invest more in AI and manage risk actively. These practices reinforce each other: redesigned workflows plus leadership, measurement and risk management create value that isolated tools do not.

notes.title: Choosing and prioritising AI use cases
notes.body: Start from business goals and pain points, not from technology. Collect ideas from each function, then score each use case on: business value (revenue, cost, risk, customer impact), feasibility (technical complexity, model capability), data readiness (is the data available, clean and allowed to be used?), risk (regulation, safety, reputation), adoption effort (how much the workflow and people must change) and time to value. Plot them on a value vs feasibility matrix: "quick wins" (high value, high feasibility) go first, "big bets" need more planning, low-value ideas are dropped. Most guidance recommends a small first wave of 2-5 use cases, often in one "lighthouse" domain, proving value and then reusing components (data pipelines, RAG platform, evaluation, guardrails) across the company. Each funded use case needs a clear value story, a baseline, an owner in the business and a defined path to production, not just a demo.

notes.title: Build, buy or partner
notes.body: For each AI capability decide whether to buy (SaaS tools, copilots), partner (vendors, system integrators, model providers) or build (your own apps, fine-tuned or custom models). Decide per component, not for the whole system. Buy when the capability is common and not a differentiator (office copilots, transcription, coding assistants): fastest and cheapest to start. Build when it is core to your competitive advantage, uses proprietary data or must be deeply integrated into your workflows. Partner to move fast while building skills. Most companies use a hybrid: buy models via APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) or use open-weight models, and build their own data, retrieval, workflows and evaluation layer on top. BCG frames the moves as adopt, partner, build and buy, where the goal is the access you need for an advantage, not maximum ownership. Watch for vendor lock-in: keep model-agnostic interfaces (gateways), own your data and prompts, and set exit criteria and regular vendor reviews.

notes.title: AI operating models: centralized, federated, hub-and-spoke
notes.body: The operating model decides who owns AI work. Centralized (AI Center of Excellence, CoE): one central team builds and governs AI; good for a fast, consistent start and scarce skills, but it becomes a bottleneck and can be far from business needs. Federated (decentralized): each business unit builds its own AI; close to the business and fast, but risks duplicated work, inconsistent data, monitoring and risk handling, and "fake federation" where units have accountability but no budget or decision rights. Hub-and-spoke (hybrid): a central hub provides platforms, standards, governance, security and shared components, while spokes (AI teams embedded in business units) own use cases and delivery. Many companies start with a CoE and move to hub-and-spoke once demand outgrows central capacity. Roles often include an executive sponsor or Chief AI Officer, product owners in the business, an AI platform team, and risk, legal and security partners.

notes.title: AI governance, responsible AI and regulation
notes.body: Governance makes AI safe, legal and trusted without stopping progress. Building blocks: an AI policy (approved tools, data rules), an inventory of AI systems, risk tiers (more review for higher-risk uses such as hiring, credit or health), human oversight rules, model evaluation and monitoring, incident response, and clear accountability. Frameworks: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (voluntary, US) organises work into four functions: Govern (culture, roles, policies; cross-cutting), Map (understand context and risks), Measure (test, evaluate, verify and validate) and Manage (prioritise, respond, monitor). ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable international standard for an AI management system. The EU AI Act sorts AI by risk: prohibited practices (in force since February 2025), high-risk systems (strict requirements; dates moved later by the 2026 "AI Omnibus"), transparency duties for chatbots and generated content, and rules for general-purpose AI models since August 2025. Always check the official timeline for current dates.

notes.title: Measuring AI value and ROI
notes.body: Measure before you build: record a baseline (time per task, cost per case, error rate, conversion, customer satisfaction). Track three layers: adoption (active users, usage per user, task completion without human rescue), operational impact (time saved, throughput, quality, cycle time) and financial impact (cost savings, revenue growth, risk reduction). Hours saved only become value if the time is redeployed or costs actually fall. ROI = (total financial value - total AI cost) / total AI cost × 100. Total cost of ownership includes more than licences: tokens and cloud compute, integration and data work, evaluation and monitoring, security and compliance, change management and training, and ongoing maintenance. Use controlled comparisons (A/B tests, pilot vs control group) to show causality. Report value regularly to leadership, and stop or rework use cases that do not deliver. Value often takes months to show, so set realistic milestones.

notes.title: People, skills and change management
notes.body: Technology is rarely the hardest part; adoption is. Effective AI strategies include: visible leadership sponsorship; AI literacy for everyone (what AI can and cannot do, safe use, data privacy), which the EU AI Act also expects from organisations that deploy AI; deeper upskilling for builders (prompting, RAG, evaluation, agents) and for managers (redesigning work); champions or "AI ambassadors" in each team; redesigned roles, incentives and processes so people actually use the tools; and honest communication about job changes, with reskilling paths. Reports suggest only a small share of organisations have a real change-management plan for AI. Partnership matters: the CEO and business leaders own outcomes, the CIO or CTO owns platforms, the CHRO owns skills and organisation design, and a Chief AI Officer (common where AI is core to the business) coordinates the strategy, portfolio and governance.

notes.title: AI maturity and roadmap
notes.body: Maturity models (for example Gartner's five-level AI maturity model) help a company see where it stands, from ad hoc experiments to AI embedded across the business, across dimensions such as strategy, data, governance, engineering, operating model, culture and value. A practical roadmap: Phase 1 (0-6 months) Foundations: set the ambition, AI policy and governance, approve safe tools, give staff AI literacy, pick 2-5 high-value use cases and set baselines. Phase 2 (6-18 months) Scale: build a shared platform (data, model access via a gateway, RAG, evaluation, monitoring), move proven pilots into production, redesign workflows, and grow a hub-and-spoke team. Phase 3 (18+ months) Transform: AI-native processes and products, agents for multi-step work, continuous value tracking and portfolio rebalancing. Review the strategy at least yearly, because models, costs and regulation change fast.

notes.title: Rewired (McKinsey): the six capabilities for tech and AI transformation
notes.body: Rewired is McKinsey's book on how companies win with digital technology and AI. The first edition (2023, Lamarre, Smaje and Zemmel) was subtitled "The McKinsey Guide to Outcompeting in the Age of Digital and AI". The second edition (Wiley, April 2026, by Eric Lamarre, Kate Smaje, Robert Levin, Alex Singla and Alexander Sukharevsky) updates it for generative and agentic AI, drawing on more than 200 enterprise-wide transformations and over 30 case studies. Its core is six capabilities a company must build together: 1) a business-led strategic roadmap that focuses on a few domains with big value; 2) talent: building an in-house bench of engineers, data and product people; 3) an operating model where small cross-functional agile teams own outcomes and scale; 4) technology: a distributed, modern tech stack (cloud, APIs, platforms) that lets teams ship fast; 5) data embedded everywhere, managed as reusable data products; 6) adoption and scaling: redesigning processes and roles, tracking adoption and replicating solutions across the business. Key ideas in the second edition: agentic AI means reimagining workflows end to end in targeted domains rather than adding AI to single tasks; adoption and change (process redesign, new human roles, tracking use) become a core discipline, the "how" behind AI's "wow"; and companies that built these capabilities in the first AI wave are pulling further ahead.

notes.title: MCP in 2026: governance, versions and what changed
notes.body: The Model Context Protocol (MCP), launched by Anthropic in November 2024, is an open standard that lets AI apps (hosts) connect to tools and data through servers. A host runs one client per server; servers expose tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts (templates) over JSON-RPC. The spec is versioned by date: 2024-11-05 (first release), 2025-03-26 (Streamable HTTP transport and OAuth-based authorization), 2025-06-18 (structured tool output and elicitation, where a server asks the user for input) and 2025-11-25 (async tasks for long-running work and an extensions system, among other changes). In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a fund hosted by the Linux Foundation and co-founded with OpenAI and Block, so changes now go through public Specification Enhancement Proposals (SEPs). Later 2026 revisions continue to simplify the protocol; check modelcontextprotocol.io for the current version. Practical lesson: pin the spec version your client and server support, and prefer remote servers with OAuth over sharing long-lived API keys.

notes.title: A2A vs MCP: agent-to-agent vs agent-to-tool
notes.body: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol, first introduced by Google in 2025 and now a Linux Foundation project, for one AI agent to discover and delegate work to another. Each agent publishes an Agent Card, a JSON document usually at /.well-known/agent.json, listing its skills, accepted input and output types and how to authenticate. Work is sent as a Task, which moves through states such as submitted, working, input-required and completed; long jobs report progress by streaming or push notifications. A2A runs over HTTP and JSON-RPC. MCP solves a different problem: connecting one agent to tools and data (databases, APIs, files). A simple rule: use MCP when an agent needs a capability, and A2A when it needs a colleague. Many systems use both: an agent uses MCP internally to read its database, then uses A2A to ask a supplier's agent to place an order. Security matters for both: verify agent identity, limit what a delegated agent may do and log every hand-off.

notes.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
notes.body: The OWASP GenAI Security Project publishes the most-used list of risks for LLM applications. The 2025 edition: LLM01 Prompt Injection (inputs, including hidden text in documents or web pages, change the model's behaviour); LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure; LLM03 Supply Chain (unsafe models, datasets or plugins); LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning; LLM05 Improper Output Handling (passing model output to a browser, shell or SQL without validation); LLM06 Excessive Agency (too many tools or permissions); LLM07 System Prompt Leakage (new); LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (new, for RAG); LLM09 Misinformation (confident wrong answers); LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (runaway cost or denial of service). Core defences: treat all model output as untrusted, give least privilege to tools, keep secrets out of prompts, filter retrieved content by user permissions, require human approval for risky actions, rate-limit and set budgets, and red-team before launch.

notes.title: Securing AI agents: OWASP agentic risks and the lethal trifecta
notes.body: In December 2025 OWASP released a separate Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01-ASI10), because agents that plan and act bring new risks. They include agent goal hijacking (an attacker redirects the agent through injected instructions), tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply-chain risks, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure agent-to-agent communication, cascading failures, exploitation of human trust and rogue agents. A useful mental model is the "lethal trifecta": an agent that has access to private data, reads untrusted content (web pages, emails, documents) and can communicate externally can be tricked into leaking data. Remove at least one of the three for risky tasks. Other defences: sandbox code execution, give each agent its own scoped identity and short-lived credentials, allow-list tools and destinations, require confirmation for irreversible actions, cap loops and spending, and log every tool call for audit.

notes.title: EU AI Act: risk tiers and the timeline after the Digital Omnibus
notes.body: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024 and sorts AI by risk. Unacceptable-risk practices (for example social scoring and some manipulative or biometric uses) have been banned since 2 February 2025, together with an AI literacy duty. Obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers (technical documentation, copyright policy, training-data summary, and extra duties for models with systemic risk) apply from 2 August 2025. High-risk systems (in areas such as hiring, credit scoring, education, essential services and law enforcement) need risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and conformity assessment. In 2026 the EU adopted the Digital Omnibus on AI, which delayed the high-risk rules: stand-alone Annex III systems moved from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and AI inside regulated products (Annex I) to 2 August 2028. Prohibitions, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency rules (telling people they are talking to AI and labelling deepfakes) were not delayed. Fines reach up to 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices.

notes.title: AI governance frameworks: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
notes.body: Companies rarely build governance from scratch; they map to frameworks. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, January 2023, voluntary, US) has four functions: Govern (culture, policies, roles and accountability), Map (understand the context, intended use and impacts), Measure (test and track risks such as bias, robustness and privacy) and Manage (prioritise, respond and monitor). NIST added a Generative AI Profile in July 2024 covering risks such as confabulation and harmful content. ISO/IEC 42001 (December 2023) is a certifiable management-system standard for AI, similar in style to ISO 27001 for security: it requires an AI policy, risk and impact assessments, controls and continual improvement. A practical governance programme combines them: keep an inventory of AI systems, classify each by risk (aligned to the EU AI Act if you operate in the EU), assign an owner, define required testing and human review per risk tier, record decisions and incidents, and review regularly.

notes.title: Context engineering techniques: compaction, notes, sub-agents and just-in-time retrieval
notes.body: Context engineering is curating the smallest set of high-signal tokens the model sees at each step. It matters because recall gets worse as the context fills ("context rot"), even inside large windows. Main techniques: (1) Compaction: when the conversation nears the limit, summarise it and continue from the summary; the lightest form is clearing old raw tool results once they have been used. (2) Structured note-taking: the agent writes progress, decisions and to-do lists to a file (for example NOTES.md) outside the context and reads it back later, which supports long tasks. (3) Sub-agents: a lead agent hands focused tasks to sub-agents with clean context windows; each may use tens of thousands of tokens but returns a short summary. (4) Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (file paths, URLs, queries) and load data only when needed instead of stuffing everything up front. Also: write system prompts at the right altitude (clear but not brittle), keep tools few, distinct and token-efficient, and use a small set of canonical examples rather than a long list of edge cases.

notes.title: Agent harnesses: Agent = Model + Harness
notes.body: A harness is all the software around a model that turns it into an agent. A popular formula from 2026 is Agent = Model + Harness. Coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and OpenHands are harnesses wrapped around LLMs. Typical parts: the control loop (call the model, run the tools it asks for, feed results back, repeat until done); tools (read and edit files, run shell commands, search the web); permissions and sandboxes (what the agent may do without asking); context management (compaction, memory files such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, retrieval); sub-agents for parallel or isolated work; hooks and skills that add project rules; and recovery paths when a step fails. Studies show the harness changes results a lot: the same model can score very differently with different harnesses, so benchmark results should name the harness. "Harness engineering" means improving these parts: better tool descriptions, tighter feedback loops (run tests after edits), safer defaults and smarter context handling.

notes.title: Benchmarks in 2026: saturation and the new hard tests
notes.body: Older benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K and HumanEval are saturated: top models score near the ceiling, so they no longer separate models. Newer, harder tests took their place. Humanity's Last Exam (HLE, from the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, 2025) has about 2,500 expert-written questions across many subjects, designed to resist web search. ARC-AGI-2 tests abstract visual reasoning that is easy for people but hard for models; ARC-AGI-3 (2026) moves to interactive games. SWE-bench Verified and the harder SWE-bench Pro test fixing real software issues. METR's time-horizon measure asks how long a task (in human working time) an AI agent can complete with 50% success; it has been doubling roughly every 4-7 months. Scores differ between leaderboards because of settings, tools, harnesses and contamination, and some public tasks turn out to be broken, so always check the official leaderboard, the exact setup and independent replications before trusting a headline number.

notes.title: Choosing a fine-tuning method: SFT, LoRA, QLoRA, DPO and GRPO
notes.body: Pick the method from the training signal you have. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from input-output examples and is the usual first step, for style, format, domain vocabulary or a specific task. LoRA and QLoRA are not separate goals but cheaper ways to train: LoRA freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices; QLoRA (2023) does the same on a 4-bit quantized base so a large model fits on one GPU. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization, 2023) learns from pairs of chosen and rejected answers without a separate reward model, good for tone and preferences. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, from DeepSeek, used for DeepSeek-R1) is reinforcement fine-tuning: for each prompt it samples several answers, scores them with a reward function and pushes the model toward the better ones; it suits math, code and other tasks with verifiable answers. Rules of thumb: try prompting and RAG first, start with SFT plus LoRA, use GRPO when you can grade answers automatically, and remember that data quality matters more than the algorithm. Always compare against the base model on a held-out eval set.

notes.title: Prompt engineering fundamentals that still work
notes.body: Good prompts are clear, specific and give context. Core techniques: (1) Say exactly what you want, including audience, length, format and what "done" looks like; explain why, because models follow reasons better than bare rules. (2) Give examples (few-shot) when format or style matters; vary them so the model does not copy one pattern. (3) Separate parts of a prompt with clear structure, such as XML-style tags (<document>, <instructions>) or headings, so instructions are not confused with data. (4) Let the model think: ask it to reason step by step (chain of thought) or use a reasoning model for hard problems. (5) Assign a role or put stable rules in the system prompt. (6) Ask for structured output (JSON matching a schema) when code will read the answer. (7) Break big tasks into a chain of smaller prompts. (8) Put long documents first and the question last. Treat prompts like code: keep them in version control, build a small test set and measure changes instead of judging by one example. Never put secrets in prompts, and treat retrieved text as data, not instructions.

notes.title: Generative video in 2026: native audio, longer shots and world models
notes.body: Video generation moved fast. Most frontier models are diffusion models built on transformers (diffusion transformers): they start from noise in a compressed latent space and remove it step by step, guided by the text prompt. Google's Veo 3 (announced in 2025) popularised native audio, generating dialogue, sound effects and music in the same pass as the frames, and by 2026 most leading models (for example Veo, Kling and Seedance) did the same. Other trends: higher resolution (up to 4K), multi-shot scenes with consistent characters, image-to-video and video editing, and open-weight models such as LTX. Common weaknesses remain: physics errors, morphing hands and objects, and drift in long clips. Related "world models" such as Google DeepMind's Genie 3 generate interactive environments in real time instead of fixed clips. Responsible use matters: label AI-generated media (the EU AI Act requires deepfake labelling), use content credentials such as C2PA, and respect likeness and copyright.

notes.title: The frontier AI landscape and how to follow it
notes.body: The frontier is shared by a few groups. US closed-model labs: OpenAI (GPT models, ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google DeepMind (Gemini) and xAI (Grok).
