Meta releases open-weight Llama models. Strong Chinese labs mostly release open weights: DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot AI (Kimi), Zhipu AI (GLM) and MiniMax. In Europe, Mistral AI offers both open and commercial models. New flagship versions now arrive every few months, often in families (a large reasoning model plus faster, cheaper ones). To follow releases reliably, read the lab's own announcement, model card and system card (which reports safety testing), check independent evaluations and leaderboards, and compare price per million input and output tokens, context window and rate limits. Be careful with aggregator sites: they often disagree on names and dates. For a product decision, test the candidate models on your own tasks; the "best" model on a leaderboard is not always best, or cheapest, for your use case.

notes.title: AI agents in the terminal and the shell skills behind them
notes.body: Command-line coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI and Google's open-source Gemini CLI run in a terminal, read and edit files and run shell commands for you. Most also have a non-interactive mode for scripts and CI (for example passing a prompt with a flag and printing the result), so they can review pull requests or fix failing tests automatically. To use them well you need basic shell skills: standard input and output, pipes (|) to pass one command's output to another, redirection (> to a file), exit codes (0 means success, anything else means failure), environment variables for configuration and secrets, and tools such as grep (search text), curl (send HTTP requests, often to test APIs), jq (filter JSON) and git. Safety: review the commands an agent proposes, run it in a project folder or sandbox, keep API keys in environment variables rather than in code, and use allow-lists for commands it may run without asking.

notes.title: Modern LLM families: reasoning models, MoE, SLMs, VLMs and audio models
notes.body: Today's language models come in several flavours. Reasoning models spend extra "thinking" tokens before answering (test-time compute), which improves math, coding and planning but costs more time and tokens; many APIs let you set the thinking budget. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models contain many expert sub-networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them, so a model with a huge total parameter count uses only a fraction per token, making it cheaper to run (DeepSeek, Qwen and Mixtral use MoE). Small language models (SLMs, roughly under 10B parameters) run on laptops and phones for privacy, low latency and low cost. Vision-language models (VLMs) take images (and often video) as input alongside text. Audio language models (ALMs) understand or generate speech directly, enabling real-time voice assistants. Choosing among them is a trade-off between quality, latency, cost, privacy and where the model must run.

notes.title: Estimating KV cache memory
notes.body: During generation a model stores keys and values for every past token: the KV cache. Its size often decides how many users fit on a GPU. Formula: KV bytes = 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × concurrent sequences × bytes per value. Example, Llama 3 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention), head dimension 128, FP16 (2 bytes): 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes, about 0.31 MB per token. An 8,000-token conversation therefore needs about 2.6 GB, and 32 such users about 84 GB, on top of about 140 GB for the FP16 weights. Ways to shrink it: grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads), an FP8 KV cache (half the size), paged attention (vLLM) to avoid wasted memory, prefix caching to share common prompt prefixes, and shorter context limits. Always add headroom (about 10-20%) for activations and fragmentation.

notes.title: Evaluating agents: pass@k, pass^k and trajectories
notes.body: Agents are non-deterministic, so one run proves little. Two metrics help. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds; it fits tasks where you can try several times and check (for example code with tests). pass^k (pass-hat-k, used by the tau-bench agent benchmark) is the chance that all k attempts succeed; it measures reliability, which matters for customer-facing agents where every run must work. A model can have a high pass@k but a low pass^k. Grade both the outcome (check the final state: tests pass, the database record changed) and the trajectory (right tools, valid arguments, no forbidden actions, reasonable number of steps, recovery from errors). Build the task set from real user requests, add every production failure as a new test, run each task several times, and track cost and latency alongside success. Use LLM judges only after checking them against human labels.

notes.title: World models vs game engines
notes.body: A game engine (Unreal, Unity, Godot) simulates a world from explicit assets, rules and physics code, so it is exact, repeatable and controllable. A world model learns to generate the next frames from video data and user actions. Google DeepMind's Genie 3 (August 2025) was its first world model to allow real-time interaction, at about 720p and 24 frames per second, with consistency lasting a few minutes. Open alternatives such as Skywork's Matrix-Game 2.0 were trained on gameplay footage from engines. World models are good for fast prototyping, generating varied training environments for robots and agents, and creative exploration, but they forget details, cannot guarantee exact rules and are expensive to run, so they do not replace engines for shipped games. AI already helps inside engines in other ways: neural upscaling and frame generation (such as NVIDIA DLSS), procedural content, AI-assisted coding and asset creation, and LLM-driven characters with dialogue.

notes.title: AI risk management: the lifecycle and the key frameworks
notes.body: AI risk management means finding, measuring, reducing and monitoring the ways an AI system can cause harm, to people, to the organisation or to society, across its whole life: design, data, training, testing, deployment and retirement. The main frameworks: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023) with four functions, Govern (policies, roles, accountability), Map (context, intended use, who could be affected), Measure (test and track risks) and Manage (prioritise, treat, monitor and respond); its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) adds GenAI risks such as confabulation, harmful content, data privacy and information integrity. ISO/IEC 23894 (2023) applies the general ISO 31000 risk process to AI, and ISO/IEC 42001 adds a certifiable AI management system. Regulations such as the EU AI Act turn risk management into a legal duty for high-risk systems. A typical process: inventory every AI system, classify each by risk tier, assess likelihood and impact, choose controls, assign an owner, document the decision, and monitor with key risk indicators.

notes.title: A taxonomy of AI risks: what can go wrong
notes.body: The MIT AI Risk Repository collects hundreds of risks from published AI frameworks and groups them into seven domains: (1) discrimination and toxicity (bias, unfair outcomes, harmful content); (2) privacy and security (leaking personal data, attacks on models, prompt injection); (3) misinformation (false or misleading output, pollution of the information ecosystem); (4) malicious actors and misuse (fraud, cyberattacks, weapons, surveillance); (5) human-computer interaction (over-reliance, loss of human agency); (6) socioeconomic and environmental harms (job impacts, concentration of power, energy use); (7) AI system safety, failures and limitations (wrong answers, lack of robustness, models pursuing unintended goals). It also classifies risks by cause: whether a human or the AI causes them, whether intentional or not, and whether they appear before or after deployment. Using a shared taxonomy helps a risk team check that its assessment has not missed a whole category.

notes.title: Practical controls for AI risk
notes.body: Banks have managed model risk for years under guidance such as the US Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 (2011): independent validation, clear documentation, ongoing monitoring and a model inventory. The same ideas extend to AI. Common controls: (1) data controls (lineage, consent, quality checks, removing personal data); (2) testing before launch (accuracy on representative data, bias and fairness tests across groups, robustness, red-teaming for misuse and prompt injection); (3) human oversight proportional to impact (human review for high-stakes decisions, clear escalation paths); (4) technical guardrails (input and output filters, least-privilege tools for agents, rate and spending limits); (5) transparency (model cards, telling users they are dealing with AI, explanations for decisions); (6) monitoring after launch (drift, error rates, complaints and incidents, with thresholds that trigger review or rollback); (7) third-party risk (due diligence on AI vendors, contracts on data use, retention and incident notice). Track key risk indicators such as error rate, override rate, complaint rate and incident count, and review them on a schedule.

notes.title: AI incidents, red-teaming and risk appetite
notes.body: Learning from failures is central to AI risk management. The AI Incident Database records thousands of real cases where AI caused or nearly caused harm, such as biased decisions, false arrests from face recognition, chatbots giving dangerous advice and deepfake fraud; reviewing similar incidents is a quick way to find risks for a new project. Red-teaming means deliberately attacking your own system before others do, through jailbreaks, prompt injection, data extraction and misuse scenarios, by internal teams, external experts or automated tools. Every organisation should also define its risk appetite: which uses are prohibited, which need extra approval and which are low-risk enough to proceed quickly. Residual risk is what remains after controls; a named owner must formally accept it. Finally, prepare an AI incident response plan: how to detect a problem, who decides to pause or roll back the system, how to notify affected people and regulators, and how lessons feed back into testing.

notes.title: AI incidents: security breaches and hacks
notes.body: Notable AI security incidents: (1) Samsung, April 2023: engineers pasted confidential source code and meeting notes into ChatGPT; Samsung then restricted generative AI tools at work. (2) ChatGPT, March 2023: a bug in an open-source library briefly showed some users other people's chat titles and partial payment details. (3) Bing Chat, February 2023: users used prompt injection to make it reveal its hidden "Sydney" system prompt. (4) DeepSeek, January 2025: researchers at Wiz found a publicly exposed database containing chat logs and API secrets. (5) EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), June 2025: a zero-click prompt-injection flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot where a crafted email could make Copilot send internal data to an attacker; rated critical (CVSS 9.3) and fixed server-side, with no known customer impact. (6) Amazon Q Developer, July 2025: an attacker got a destructive "wiper" prompt merged into the VS Code extension through a pull request; Amazon removed it and said no customer resources were affected. (7) Salesloft Drift, August 2025: attackers stole OAuth tokens from the Drift AI chat agent's Salesforce integration and exported data from hundreds of organisations. (8) November 2025: Anthropic reported that a state-linked group misused Claude Code to run a largely automated cyber-espionage campaign. Lessons: treat prompts and AI output as untrusted, protect integrations and tokens, review code contributions and limit agent permissions.

notes.title: AI incidents: agent and product failures
notes.body: When AI products fail in public: (1) Microsoft Tay, 2016: a Twitter chatbot learned offensive language from users and was shut down within a day. (2) Zillow Offers, 2021: the home-price algorithm overpaid for houses; Zillow closed the business with large losses and job cuts. (3) Google Bard launch, February 2023: a demo answer wrongly claimed the James Webb telescope took the first exoplanet picture, and Alphabet's market value fell by about $100 billion that day. (4) Chevrolet dealer chatbot, December 2023: users tricked it into "agreeing" to sell a car for $1. (5) Google Gemini images, February 2024: Google paused people images after historically inaccurate results. (6) Air Canada, February 2024: a tribunal held the airline liable after its chatbot invented a bereavement refund policy; the company had argued the bot was responsible for its own words. (7) New York City MyCity chatbot, 2024: gave business owners advice that broke the law. (8) Google AI Overviews, May 2024: suggested adding glue to pizza sauce, based on a joke forum post. (9) Replit, July 2025: an AI coding agent deleted a company's production database during a code freeze. Lessons: companies are responsible for what their AI says, test edge cases and adversarial users, and never give agents unreviewed access to production.

notes.title: AI incidents: hallucinations in professional work
notes.body: Fabricated facts have caused real damage. Mata v. Avianca (New York, 2023): lawyers filed a brief citing six court cases that ChatGPT invented; the judge fined them $5,000. Since then courts in many countries have sanctioned lawyers for AI-invented citations, and researchers track hundreds of such cases. Deloitte Australia (2025): a government report contained fabricated references and quotes produced with generative AI; Deloitte corrected the report and refunded part of its fee. Other cases include AI-generated summaries and articles with invented quotes, and medical or legal chatbots giving confident wrong answers. Lessons: verify every citation, quote and number against the original source; require human review and sign-off for professional work; disclose AI use where rules require it; and prefer tools that retrieve and cite real documents.

notes.title: AI incidents: bias and discrimination
notes.body: Well-known bias cases: (1) COMPAS (US, 2016): a ProPublica investigation found the criminal risk-scoring tool falsely flagged Black defendants as high-risk more often than white defendants. (2) Amazon recruiting tool (reported 2018): it learned to downgrade CVs that mentioned women's activities, and Amazon scrapped it. (3) Netherlands childcare benefits scandal: a risk algorithm and practices wrongly accused thousands of families, many with dual nationality, of fraud; the Dutch government resigned in January 2021. (4) UK A-level grades, 2020: an algorithm downgraded many students from disadvantaged schools and was withdrawn after protests. (5) Robert Williams, Detroit, 2020: wrongfully arrested after a face-recognition false match, one of several such US cases. (6) iTutorGroup, 2023: settled a US EEOC case for $365,000 after its hiring software automatically rejected older applicants. (7) Mobley v. Workday: a US lawsuit alleging AI screening discriminated by age, race and disability, allowed to proceed as a collective action in 2025. Lessons: test outcomes across groups before and after launch, keep humans accountable for decisions, and give people a way to appeal.

notes.title: AI incidents: deepfakes and fraud
notes.body: Generative AI has made impersonation cheap. (1) 2019: criminals used a cloned voice of a parent-company chief executive to trick a UK energy firm into transferring about €220,000. (2) Arup, Hong Kong, early 2024: an employee transferred about US$25 million after a video call in which the CFO and colleagues were all deepfakes. (3) New Hampshire, January 2024: robocalls with a fake Joe Biden voice told people not to vote in the primary; the US FCC fined the political consultant behind them $6 million and banned AI voices in robocalls without consent. (4) January 2024: sexually explicit deepfakes of Taylor Swift spread widely on X, which temporarily blocked searches for her name. Since then, deepfake scams using cloned voices of relatives or executives have grown fast. Defences: verify payment requests through a second known channel, use code words for urgent requests, train staff, label AI media and use content credentials such as C2PA.

notes.title: AI incidents: lawsuits and regulatory actions
notes.body: Key legal cases: (1) Italy, March 2023: the data-protection authority temporarily banned ChatGPT, and in December 2024 fined OpenAI €15 million over privacy issues. (2) The New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft (filed December 2023): copyright claims over training on and reproducing news articles. (3) US FTC v. Rite Aid, December 2023: Rite Aid was banned from using facial recognition for five years after false matches harmed shoppers. (4) Clearview AI: fined by several European regulators for scraping faces without consent. (5) Garcia v. Character Technologies (October 2024) and Raine v. OpenAI (August 2025): families sued chatbot makers after teenagers' suicides, pushing new safety features for minors. (6) Disney and Universal v. Midjourney (June 2025): copyright claims over generated images of their characters. (7) Bartz v. Anthropic: a $1.5 billion settlement (2025) over books obtained from pirate sites for training. (8) Getty Images v. Stability AI (UK High Court, 4 November 2025): Getty lost its main copyright claims and won only a narrow trademark point; an appeal was allowed. (9) Amazon v. Perplexity (November 2025): over the Comet browser's AI agent shopping on Amazon. Lessons: know where training data comes from, respect privacy law, and build safety for vulnerable users.

notes.title: AI incidents: autonomous vehicles and physical safety
notes.body: AI in the physical world raises the stakes. (1) Uber, Tempe, Arizona, March 2018: a self-driving test car killed pedestrian Elaine Herzberg, the first pedestrian death involving a self-driving car; the safety driver was distracted and the system failed to classify her correctly in time. (2) Cruise, San Francisco, October 2023: a robotaxi dragged a pedestrian who had been thrown into its path by another car; California suspended Cruise's permits, and GM later stopped its robotaxi programme. (3) Tesla Autopilot and Full Self-Driving: many crashes have been investigated by US regulators, and in August 2025 a Florida jury found Tesla partly liable for a 2019 crash, awarding damages of over $200 million. Lessons: safety cases and independent testing before deployment, honest communication about limits, driver-monitoring for partial automation, and fast transparent incident reporting to regulators.

notes.title: Transformers and attention: the core ideas
notes.body: The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need") replaced recurrence with attention, so every token in a sequence can look at every other token in parallel. Self-attention turns each token into three vectors: a query, a key and a value. Each token scores every other token by the dot product of its query with their keys, divides by the square root of the key size, applies softmax to get weights, and takes the weighted sum of the values. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel so different heads can learn different relationships. Because attention has no built-in sense of order, positional information is added (sine/cosine encodings in the original paper; learned or rotary embeddings in many later models). Each layer also has a feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalisation. The original design had an encoder and a decoder; BERT uses only the encoder, and GPT-style LLMs use only the decoder with causal masking so a token cannot see future tokens. Attention cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which is why long context is expensive and why techniques such as the KV cache and FlashAttention matter.

notes.title: Running models locally: Ollama and multi-provider chat apps
notes.body: Ollama is a free, open-source tool that runs open-weight models on your own computer. One command, such as "ollama run llama3.2", downloads a model and starts a chat. It can run models from many different makers (Meta Llama, Google Gemma, Alibaba Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek and others), and it serves them through a local API on port 11434 that also speaks the OpenAI API format, so many apps written for OpenAI can point at your own machine instead. Local models are usually quantized (for example to 4-bit), which shrinks memory use so they fit on a laptop or consumer GPU at a small cost in quality. Benefits of local hosting: your data stays on your machine, it works offline and there are no per-token fees; the trade-offs are that you need capable hardware and the biggest frontier models are not available. On top of Ollama or cloud APIs you can run a self-hosted chat interface: Open WebUI works with Ollama and OpenAI-compatible APIs, and LibreChat connects to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others, so one screen can switch between local and cloud models using your own API keys ("bring your own key"). A chat client is the user interface; a model gateway such as OpenRouter is an API that routes requests to many models.

notes.title: OpenClaw: what it is and how it works
notes.body: OpenClaw is a free, open-source personal AI agent that you run yourself, on your own computer, a small cloud server or an old desktop. Unlike a chatbot in a browser tab, it is always on and can act for you. A central Gateway process keeps connections to messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram, so you talk to the same assistant from your phone. Each message is passed to an AI model (you choose and pay for the model), which can use tools such as the shell, the browser, files and calendars, and the reply comes back through the same chat app. Its abilities are extended with skills: a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions (and optional scripts), loaded only when needed; skills are shared on the ClawHub marketplace. Memory is kept as plain Markdown files on disk rather than in a database, so you can read and edit what it remembers. A heartbeat timer wakes the agent regularly (every 30 minutes by default in common setups) to check a HEARTBEAT.md task list and act without being asked, which makes it proactive.

notes.title: OpenClaw history: Clawdbot, Moltbot and Moltbook
notes.body: OpenClaw was created by the Austrian developer Peter Steinberger, as a quick weekend project to send prompts from his phone (through WhatsApp) to an AI coding agent on his Mac. It was first called Clawdbot, with a lobster mascot. In January 2026 Anthropic raised a trademark concern because "Clawd" sounded too much like "Claude", so it was renamed Moltbot (lobsters molt, or shed their shell) and, days later, OpenClaw. During the rename, scammers grabbed the abandoned social media handle to promote a fake crypto token, an early sign of how much attention the project drew. It became one of the fastest-growing projects in GitHub history. Also in late January 2026, Matt Schlicht launched Moltbook, a Reddit-style social network where only AI agents (mostly OpenClaw agents) post, comment and vote while humans watch; critics noted that humans still prompt the agents and that many posts could be steered by people. In February 2026 Steinberger announced he was joining OpenAI to work on agents, while OpenClaw stays open source.

notes.title: OpenClaw security: skills, exposed servers and the lethal trifecta
notes.body: Because OpenClaw can read your messages, files and accounts and can run commands, mistakes are costly. Three lessons from 2026: (1) Skill supply-chain attacks: security firm Koi Security audited ClawHub in early February 2026 and flagged 341 malicious skills, most from one coordinated campaign named ClawHavoc; many posed as crypto or productivity tools and tricked users into installing info-stealing malware. ClawHub then added VirusTotal scanning. Treat a skill like any software you install: check the author, read the SKILL.md and scripts, and prefer well-known skills. (2) Exposed instances: researchers found tens of thousands of OpenClaw control panels reachable from the internet, and a one-click remote code execution bug (CVE-2026-25253) was patched in January 2026. Keep the Gateway private (bind to localhost or use a VPN), keep it updated and use strong tokens. (3) The lethal trifecta, a term from Simon Willison: an agent that has access to private data, reads untrusted content (emails, web pages) and can communicate externally can be tricked by prompt injection into leaking your data. Reduce risk with least-privilege accounts, a separate machine or container, human approval for sensitive actions, and spending limits on the model API.

notes.title: Bots: chatbots, agents and web crawlers
notes.body: A bot is software that performs tasks automatically. Chatbots talk with people: ELIZA (1966, Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT) imitated a psychotherapist using simple pattern matching, yet many users felt it understood them, now called the ELIZA effect. Classic customer-service bots are rule-based (decision trees and keywords) or intent-based (classify the request, then follow a script); modern chatbots use large language models and can hold open-ended conversations. An AI agent goes further than a chatbot: it plans steps and uses tools to act, for example sending emails or booking meetings. Messaging platforms such as Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack and Discord let developers build bots through official bot APIs. Other bots work in the background: web crawlers (such as Googlebot, and AI crawlers that collect training data) read websites, and site owners use a robots.txt file to say which pages crawlers may visit, though obeying it is voluntary. Social bots post automatically on social media and can spread spam or misinformation, which is why sites use CAPTCHAs and bot detection.

notes.title: Confabulation: when AI confidently makes things up
notes.body: Confabulation is when a generative AI model produces confidently stated content that is false or not supported by facts, such as invented quotes, statistics, court cases, citations or product features. It is the same problem people usually call "hallucination", and the NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) uses the word confabulation for it, listing it among the main risks of generative AI. The term comes from psychology and neurology, where it describes patients (for example with Korsakoff syndrome or certain brain injuries) who fill gaps in memory with made-up details while honestly believing them, with no intent to deceive. Many researchers prefer it to "hallucination" because the model is not perceiving something that is not there; it is filling gaps with plausible text. Why it happens: a language model predicts likely next words, not checked facts, and training and benchmarks that score only right or wrong answers reward guessing over saying "I don't know" (as OpenAI explained in September 2025). Confabulation is most likely for rare facts, recent events, exact numbers, quotes and references. Two kinds are often named: intrinsic (the output contradicts the source it was given) and extrinsic (it adds details that cannot be verified from the source). Real cases include lawyers in Mata v. Avianca (2023) citing court cases ChatGPT invented and the Air Canada chatbot inventing a refund policy (2024). How to reduce it: ground answers in retrieved sources (RAG) and ask for citations you can check; tell the model it may say it does not know; ask for quotes from the provided documents before answering; check important facts, numbers and references yourself; use human review for high-stakes outputs; and measure it with faithfulness or groundedness evaluations. Lowering the temperature makes outputs more consistent but does not stop confabulation, because a model can repeat the same false answer every time.

notes.title: Tech stacks and full-stack development
notes.body: A stack (or tech stack) is the set of technologies an app is built with, for example React for the screens, Node.js for the server logic and PostgreSQL for the data. An app usually has three layers. The frontend (client side) is what users see and click in the browser or mobile app, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, often with a framework such as React, Vue or Angular. The backend (server side) runs behind it: it holds the business logic, checks who the user is, talks to other services and AI model APIs, and is written with tools such as Node.js, Python (Django, FastAPI), Java (Spring) or C# (.NET). The database stores the data, for example PostgreSQL or MySQL (relational, tables and SQL) or MongoDB (documents). The frontend and backend usually talk through an API over HTTP, often sending JSON. Well-known stacks have short names: LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP), MERN (MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js) and MEAN (the same with Angular). Full stack means working on every layer: the frontend users see, the backend that runs behind it, and the database. A full-stack developer can build a whole feature end to end, while frontend or backend specialists go deeper on one layer. In AI apps, the model is usually called from the backend, so API keys stay secret on the server and never reach the browser; AI coding tools now help one person build a full-stack app much faster.

notes.title: Arduino vs Raspberry Pi
notes.body: Arduino is a small, cheap microcontroller board you program in C/C++ to control electronics directly, such as reading sensors, turning on LEDs or driving motors. Unlike a Raspberry Pi, it has no operating system: it runs one program in a loop, starts instantly and uses very little power. An Arduino program is called a sketch: setup() runs once at power-on and loop() then repeats forever. A Raspberry Pi is a small single-board computer: it runs a full operating system (usually Linux), has far more memory and processing power, and can run many programs at once, connect a screen, keyboard and network, and run Python or even small AI models. In short: use an Arduino for simple, reliable, low-power control of hardware in real time; use a Raspberry Pi when you need a real computer, such as running a web server, a camera with image recognition or a local AI model. Many projects use both, with the Pi doing the thinking and the Arduino handling the sensors and motors.

notes.title: When to fine-tune, and what can go wrong
notes.body: Fine-tuning means further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so it adapts to a task. Try the cheaper options first: a better prompt, then retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for knowledge, and fine-tune only when those fall short. Rule of thumb: RAG is better for facts that change (policies, prices, product data) because you just update the documents; fine-tuning is better for a consistent style, tone, output format or a narrow skill, and for making a small model do one job as well as a big one. Main options: full fine-tuning updates every weight (best quality, most memory); parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) such as LoRA freezes the base model and trains small adapter matrices, where the rank r sets their size (higher r means more trainable parameters and capacity, but more memory); QLoRA does the same on a 4-bit quantized base model. A trained LoRA adapter can be kept separate (so one base model serves many adapters) or merged into the base weights, which removes the extra adapter step so inference is as fast as the base model. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to copy a larger teacher model's outputs, a common way to make cheap, fast models. Risks: catastrophic forgetting (the model loses skills it had before, reduced by mixing in general data and using LoRA), overfitting on a small dataset, copying errors or bias from bad training examples, and weakening the model's safety behaviour. Always keep a held-out test set and compare against the base model before and after.

notes.title: EU AI Act roles, human oversight and fines
notes.body: The EU AI Act gives different duties to different roles. The provider develops an AI system (or has it developed) and places it on the market under its own name; it carries most obligations for high-risk systems, such as risk management, data quality, technical documentation, logging, conformity assessment and CE marking. The deployer is any organization using an AI system under its authority, for example a bank using a credit-scoring tool; deployers must use the system as instructed, assign trained people for human oversight, monitor it and keep logs, and some (such as public bodies) must do a fundamental rights impact assessment. Under Article 25 a deployer, importer or distributor becomes the provider if it puts its own name or trademark on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification to it, or changes a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk. Human oversight means trained people can understand the system's limits, monitor it, interpret its output, and override or stop it. Fines (Article 99) go up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for most other obligations, and up to €7.5 million or 1% for giving incorrect information to authorities. In practice, good governance starts with an AI inventory (every AI system in use with its owner, purpose, data and risk level), clear accountability, policies for acceptable use, and regular review.

notes.title: Attacks on AI models: poisoning, extraction and inference
notes.body: Beyond prompt injection, AI systems face attacks on the model and its data. Jailbreaks are prompts crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules (role-play, "ignore previous instructions", encoding tricks); prompt injection instead smuggles instructions into the app, often indirectly through web pages, emails or documents the AI reads. Data poisoning plants harmful examples in training or fine-tuning data to change behaviour or add a hidden backdoor triggered by a keyword. In October 2025 Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute showed that about 250 poisoned documents were enough to backdoor models from 600M to 13B parameters, regardless of model size: what mattered was the number of documents, not their share of the data (the test backdoor only produced gibberish, and it is unclear whether this holds for much larger models). Model extraction (model stealing) sends many queries to a model API and trains a copy from the answers. Membership inference tries to learn whether a specific record, such as a patient file, was in the training data, a privacy risk. Model inversion tries to reconstruct training data from outputs. MITRE ATLAS is a public knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on MITRE ATT&CK, used for threat modelling and red teaming. Defences: vet and track training data sources, rate-limit and monitor APIs, filter inputs and outputs, give agents least privilege, and red-team before release.

notes.title: More prompting techniques: templates, chaining, self-consistency and caching
notes.body: Zero-shot prompting asks for a task with no examples; few-shot adds a few examples. Role prompting ("You are an experienced tax accountant") shapes tone and focus. A prompt template is a reusable prompt with placeholders such as {customer_name} filled in for each request, so prompts stay consistent and testable. Prompt chaining splits a big task into steps where each prompt's output feeds the next (for example extract facts, then draft, then check), which is easier to debug than one giant prompt. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) samples several chain-of-thought answers at a non-zero temperature and picks the most common final answer, improving accuracy on maths and logic at higher cost. Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processed start (prefix) of a prompt, cutting cost and latency, but only if that prefix is identical: put stable content such as instructions, tool definitions, examples and long documents first, and the changing user question last. Other habits that work: be specific about the goal, audience and format; give the model permission to say it does not know; ask for structured output such as JSON when code will read it; and test prompts against a fixed set of examples whenever you change them.

notes.title: Agent frameworks compared
notes.body: An agent framework gives developers ready-made building blocks for tool calling, memory, multi-step loops, multi-agent coordination, tracing and human approval, so they do not have to write the agent loop from scratch. Popular options: LangGraph (from LangChain) models a workflow as a graph of nodes and edges passing shared state, supports loops, and saves checkpoints so a run can pause for human approval and resume. CrewAI organizes a "crew" of role-based agents (such as researcher, writer and reviewer) that work through tasks. The OpenAI Agents SDK (March 2025) is a lightweight successor to OpenAI's experimental Swarm project, built on agents, tools, handoffs (one agent passing control to another) and guardrails. Microsoft Agent Framework (announced October 2025, 1.0 in April 2026) unifies AutoGen and Semantic Kernel into one open-source SDK for .NET and Python; the older two are now in maintenance mode. Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK, April 2025) is an open-source framework for multi-agent systems. The Claude Agent SDK exposes the harness behind Claude Code. Agents connect to tools through MCP and to other agents through A2A. Choosing: start simple (one agent, a few tools), add human-in-the-loop checkpoints for risky actions such as payments or deleting data, and pick the framework that fits your language and cloud.

notes.title: Frontier safety frameworks: RSP, Preparedness and FSF
notes.body: The leading labs publish frameworks that say which dangerous capabilities they test for and what safeguards they add as models get stronger. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) uses AI Safety Levels (ASL-1 to ASL-4 and above), loosely modelled on biosafety levels. In May 2025 Anthropic released Claude Opus 4 with ASL-3 safeguards (stronger security for the model weights and targeted defences against help with chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons) as a precaution, because it could no longer clearly rule out that the model needed them, while Claude Sonnet 4 stayed at ASL-2. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework tracks categories such as biological and chemical, cybersecurity and AI self-improvement, with "High" and "Critical" capability thresholds that require safeguards before deployment. Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework (May 2024, updated in 2025 and 2026) is built around Critical Capability Levels (CCLs): when evaluations show a model is near a CCL, stronger security and deployment mitigations apply; later versions added a harmful-manipulation CCL and lower "tracked" levels for earlier warning. These frameworks are voluntary company policies, but laws such as the EU AI Act's rules for general-purpose AI models increasingly expect similar risk assessments.

Lists of keywords extracted from text

options: To keep context that spans chunk boundaries

By running attention on the CPU

questions.prompt: Which LLM-system pattern validates and filters model outputs (for example, schema checks or safety filters) before they reach users?

questions.prompt: Rule #1 of Google's Rules of ML is: do not be afraid to launch a product without machine learning.

questions.prompt: Starting from a pretrained model and adapting it to a new task is called:

questions.prompt: Which company develops the Llama family of open-weight models?

questions.prompt: What is context engineering?

Training a model on longer documents
Increasing the context window size in hardware
Writing one perfect system prompt and never changing it

questions.prompt: The "Lost in the Middle" paper found that LLMs use information best when it is placed:

questions.prompt: "Context rot" refers to model performance degrading as the amount of input in the context grows.

questions.prompt: When an agent nears its context limit, what does compaction do?

questions.answer: Summarizes the history and continues in a fresh context with that summary

questions.prompt: In just-in-time retrieval, an agent keeps lightweight references (like file paths) and loads the data with tools only when needed.
questions.explanation: This avoids filling the context with data up front.

questions.prompt: Why does the Manus team advise keeping the prompt prefix stable and the context append-only?

To make the model forget old tools
questions.answer: To maximize the KV-cache hit rate, which cuts latency and cost
questions.explanation: Any change early in the prompt invalidates the cached prefix for everything after it.

questions.prompt: Which failure is it when a hallucination or error enters the context and is then repeatedly referenced?
questions.explanation: Drew Breunig lists poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash as the ways long contexts fail.

questions.prompt: Using sub-agents with their own clean context windows can keep the main agent's context focused.
questions.explanation: Sub-agents explore deeply and return only a condensed result.

questions.prompt: In AI agents, what is the "harness"?

The evaluation benchmark used to score the model
questions.answer: The software around the model that runs the loop, tools, context and permissions
questions.explanation: The model decides; the harness executes tool calls, manages state and enforces limits.

questions.explanation: This loop is the core of most agent harnesses.

questions.prompt: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

questions.prompt: What is EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness used for?
options: Running standard benchmarks against language models

questions.prompt: What does SWE-bench measure?
options: Whether a system can resolve real GitHub issues so that the tests pass
Speed of code completion in an IDE
How well a model explains code in plain English
questions.answer: Whether a system can resolve real GitHub issues so that the tests pass

questions.prompt: Sandboxing in an agent harness (restricting file system and network access) limits the damage a wrong or manipulated agent action can do.
questions.explanation: Permissions and sandboxes are the main safety layer around tool execution.

questions.prompt: For agents that work across many context windows, what does Anthropic recommend the harness keep outside the context?
options: Progress notes and state files (plus git history) that the next session reads
The full raw transcript pasted into every prompt
Nothing: start each session from scratch
questions.answer: Progress notes and state files (plus git history) that the next session reads

questions.prompt: Which company makes Claude Code, an agentic coding tool that runs in the terminal?

questions.prompt: Codex CLI, an open-source terminal coding agent, comes from which company?

questions.prompt: What file in a project root does Claude Code read for project instructions and memory?

questions.prompt: What is AGENTS.md?

A list of contributors to the project
questions.answer: An open format file that gives coding agents project instructions

questions.prompt: Which Claude Code flag runs a single prompt non-interactively, prints the result and exits (useful in scripts and CI)?

questions.prompt: Aider is an open-source AI pair-programming tool that works in the terminal with your git repository.

questions.prompt: In MCP, which component exposes tools, resources and prompts?

questions.prompt: MCP servers can run locally over stdio or remotely over HTTP.
questions.explanation: stdio suits local servers; Streamable HTTP suits remote ones.

questions.prompt: What does the MCP "sampling" feature let a server do?

Run its own copy of the model locally
Stream logs back to the client
Choose which tools the client may call

Trains the worker models on the task
Runs all subtasks itself in one long context
Votes on which worker answer is best
questions.answer: Breaks the task into subtasks and delegates them to worker LLMs

questions.prompt: What is the open protocol (introduced by Google in 2025) that lets AI agents communicate with other agents?

questions.prompt: Which security principle best limits the damage a compromised or manipulated agent can do?

Use a stronger system prompt telling it to behave
Use a larger, more capable model
Turn off logging to protect privacy
questions.answer: Least privilege: give it only the tools and permissions it needs
questions.explanation: Combine with sandboxing and human approval for risky actions.

questions.prompt: An AI agent lets the LLM decide its own next steps and tool calls, instead of following a fixed code path.

questions.prompt: What is a golden dataset in LLM evaluation?
options: Representative inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria
The results from a public leaderboard
A random sample of production logs without labels
questions.answer: Representative inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria
questions.explanation: It lets you measure quality consistently before each release.

questions.prompt: Which is a known bias of LLM-as-a-judge evaluators?
options: Position bias: favoring the answer shown first
Penalizing any answer that cites sources
questions.answer: Position bias: favoring the answer shown first

questions.prompt: Offline evals run on a fixed dataset before release; online evals measure quality on live traffic.
questions.explanation: Use both: offline to catch regressions, online to see real behavior.

questions.prompt: In RAG evaluation, what does "faithfulness" measure?

How fast the answer was generated
How many documents are in the index

questions.explanation: An unfaithful answer adds claims the sources do not support.

questions.prompt: Exact-match scoring is a reliable metric for open-ended text generation like summaries.

questions.prompt: What is the practice called of reading many real model outputs to find and categorize failure modes?

questions.prompt: Why should you compare an LLM judge's grades with human labels before relying on it?

To make the judge run faster
To lower the cost per evaluation
So the judge can be fine-tuned on the labels

questions.explanation: A judge that disagrees with experts gives misleading scores.

questions.prompt: What does pairwise evaluation ask the evaluator to do?
options: Choose the better of two outputs
Score each output on a 1-10 scale independently
Compare each output with a reference answer
Rank all outputs in the dataset at once
questions.answer: Choose the better of two outputs
questions.explanation: Pointwise evaluation scores one output at a time.

questions.prompt: What does the MMLU benchmark measure?

Coding ability on real GitHub issues
Multi-turn chat quality judged by humans

questions.prompt: Which metric gives the probability that at least one of k generated code samples passes the unit tests?

A model overfitting to its fine-tuning data
Labs running the benchmark with different prompts
questions.answer: Test questions leaking into a model's training data, inflating its score

questions.prompt: How does LMArena (Chatbot Arena) rank models?

Scores from a panel of expert judges
Exact-match on a fixed test set
questions.answer: Crowdsourced pairwise human votes turned into Elo-style ratings

questions.prompt: GPQA contains graduate-level science questions designed to be hard to answer even with web search.

The dataset is too large to run cheaply
It has leaked into models' training data
Its questions are too hard for any model
questions.answer: Top models score near the maximum, so it no longer separates them
questions.explanation: Harder benchmarks then replace it.

questions.prompt: What does MLPerf Inference measure?
options: How fast systems run standard AI workloads (throughput and latency)
How accurate chatbots are on reasoning questions
How much energy a data center uses per year
How well models translate between languages
questions.answer: How fast systems run standard AI workloads (throughput and latency)
questions.explanation: It compares hardware and software systems, not model intelligence.

questions.prompt: A high public benchmark score guarantees a model will perform well on your specific task.

questions.prompt: What does GPU stand for?

It uses less power than any other memory

The GPU driver reserves half of the memory
Weights take more space as more users connect
It makes the model less accurate

Fine-tune the model on the topic

A chatbot that pretends to be human

The set of all training images

Vector search and a reranker only

questions.answer: New tools and data sources the agent can use
questions.explanation: For example browser control, docs search or databases.

questions.prompt: What is structured note-taking for agents?
options: The agent writes notes to files outside its context so it can remember later
Saving the full chat transcript into every new prompt
Asking the user to write down key facts for the agent
Storing notes in the model's weights through fine-tuning
questions.answer: The agent writes notes to files outside its context so it can remember later
questions.explanation: Notes persist across context resets.

questions.prompt: Putting every available document into the prompt always improves answers.
questions.explanation: Irrelevant context distracts the model and costs more.

questions.prompt: What is "context distraction"?
options: The context grows so long that the model over-focuses on it instead of its training knowledge
The user switches topic in the middle of a task
Two tools in the context return conflicting answers
The model ignores instructions placed in the middle of the context
questions.answer: The context grows so long that the model over-focuses on it instead of its training knowledge
questions.explanation: One of the ways long contexts fail.

questions.prompt: What is "context clash"?
options: Conflicting information inside the same context
Two users editing the same prompt at once
The context is so long the model ignores its training knowledge
A tool returns an error instead of data
questions.answer: Conflicting information inside the same context
questions.explanation: Conflicts confuse the model's answer.

questions.prompt: Why do tool definitions count against the context budget?
options: They use tokens, and too many tools make tool selection harder
They are stored in GPU memory, not in the prompt
They are cached, so they never count after the first call
They are only read when a tool is called
questions.answer: They use tokens, and too many tools make tool selection harder
questions.explanation: Load only the tools a task needs.

questions.prompt: What is the technique called of summarizing older conversation turns to free up context space?
questions.explanation: Compaction keeps key facts while dropping detail.

questions.prompt: What does isolating context with sub-agents mean?
options: Each sub-agent works in its own context window on part of the task
Clearing the context window after every step
Encrypting the prompt so tools cannot read it
Running all agents in one shared context to save tokens
questions.answer: Each sub-agent works in its own context window on part of the task
questions.explanation: Isolation prevents one task's details from crowding another.

questions.prompt: Putting key instructions at the start or end of a long prompt can help the model follow them.
questions.explanation: Models use information in the middle of long contexts less reliably.

questions.prompt: In RAG, why retrieve only the top few relevant chunks rather than the whole knowledge base?
options: To give the model just enough high-signal context
Because vector databases can only return five results
Because models can only read one document at a time
questions.answer: To give the model just enough high-signal context
questions.explanation: Less but better context usually wins.

questions.prompt: Which message format does MCP use?
questions.explanation: Requests, responses and notifications are JSON-RPC messages.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of an MCP host?
options: An AI app such as Claude Code or an IDE
A server that exposes GitHub tools
A vector database that stores embeddings
questions.answer: An AI app such as Claude Code or an IDE
questions.explanation: Hosts contain clients that connect to servers.

questions.prompt: In MCP, each client keeps a one-to-one connection with a single server.
questions.explanation: A host can run many clients, one per server.

questions.prompt: In the evaluator-optimizer pattern, what happens?
options: One LLM generates, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop
One model trains another from scratch
Several LLMs answer in parallel and the majority wins
A router sends each input to a specialist model
questions.answer: One LLM generates, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop
questions.explanation: Useful when clear evaluation criteria exist.

questions.prompt: What is the routing pattern?
options: Classifying an input and sending it to a specialized prompt, tool or model
Sending every request to all models and merging the answers
Rotating API keys to avoid rate limits
Running steps one after another, each using the last output
questions.answer: Classifying an input and sending it to a specialized prompt, tool or model
questions.explanation: Example: send billing questions to a billing flow.

questions.prompt: What is agent memory that persists across sessions usually called (two words)?
questions.explanation: Short-term memory is the current context.

questions.prompt: What is "tool poisoning" in MCP?
options: Malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description or metadata
A tool that returns slow or incomplete results
Training data manipulated to plant a backdoor
A server that crashes when called with bad arguments
questions.answer: Malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description or metadata
questions.explanation: Only install trusted servers and review tool descriptions.

questions.prompt: Agents usually use more tokens than a single LLM call for the same request.
questions.explanation: Each loop step adds model calls and tool results.

questions.prompt: What is a handoff in a multi-agent system?
options: Passing control of the task or conversation to another agent
Restarting the agent with a fresh context
Returning the final answer to the user
Calling a tool and waiting for its result
questions.answer: Passing control of the task or conversation to another agent
questions.explanation: The OpenAI Agents SDK has handoffs as a core concept.

questions.prompt: What is regression testing for prompts and LLM apps?
options: Re-running the eval suite after changes to catch quality drops
Fitting a regression line to model scores
Testing only the new features after each change
Lowering the temperature to make outputs repeatable
questions.answer: Re-running the eval suite after changes to catch quality drops
questions.explanation: Run it in CI before every release.

questions.prompt: A clear rubric makes LLM-as-a-judge grading more consistent.
questions.explanation: Specific criteria reduce vague, noisy scores.

questions.prompt: In RAG evaluation, what does context precision measure?
options: Whether the retrieved chunks are relevant, with relevant ones ranked high
How fast the retriever returns results
Whether the answer is supported by the context
How much of the needed information was retrieved
questions.answer: Whether the retrieved chunks are relevant, with relevant ones ranked high
questions.explanation: Low precision means noisy context.

questions.prompt: In RAG evaluation, what does context recall measure?
options: Whether the retrieved context contains all the information needed
Whether retrieved chunks are ranked in the right order
Whether the answer is supported by the context
How many chunks are stored in the index
questions.answer: Whether the retrieved context contains all the information needed
questions.explanation: Low recall means missing facts.

questions.prompt: What is adversarial testing to find unsafe or harmful model behavior called?
questions.explanation: Tools like promptfoo support automated red-teaming.

questions.prompt: What is A/B testing of an LLM feature?
options: Comparing two versions on live users to see which performs better
Testing the same version on two different GPUs
Asking a judge model to pick answer A or B
Running the eval suite before and after a change
questions.answer: Comparing two versions on live users to see which performs better
questions.explanation: An online evaluation method.

questions.prompt: Why run several samples per eval case for LLMs?
options: Outputs are non-deterministic, so one sample can mislead
Because the first sample is always lower quality
To train the model on its own outputs
questions.answer: Outputs are non-deterministic, so one sample can mislead
questions.explanation: Average over samples for stable scores.

questions.prompt: Where a code-based check (like JSON schema or regex) can capture a requirement, it should be preferred over an LLM judge.
questions.explanation: Code checks are cheap, fast and deterministic.

questions.prompt: What does inter-annotator agreement measure?
options: How consistently different human labelers agree
How fast annotators label each item
How often the model agrees with human labels
How many labels each item receives
questions.answer: How consistently different human labelers agree
questions.explanation: Low agreement means the task or rubric is unclear.

questions.prompt: What is SWE-bench Verified?
options: A human-validated subset of SWE-bench tasks
A benchmark of verified math proofs
A harder version of SWE-bench with unsolved issues
A leaderboard run and verified by GitHub
questions.answer: A human-validated subset of SWE-bench tasks
questions.explanation: Verification removed unclear or unfair tasks.

questions.prompt: What does ARC-AGI test?
options: Abstract reasoning puzzles that are easy for humans but hard for AI
Coding ability on real software issues
questions.answer: Abstract reasoning puzzles that are easy for humans but hard for AI
questions.explanation: It targets generalization to new problems.

questions.prompt: What is Humanity's Last Exam?
options: A benchmark of very hard expert-level questions across many subjects
A test of whether AI can pass the bar exam
A benchmark of grade-school science questions
A safety test that checks for dangerous outputs
questions.answer: A benchmark of very hard expert-level questions across many subjects
questions.explanation: Built to stay hard as models improve.

questions.prompt: Different prompting setups, such as few-shot versus zero-shot, can change benchmark scores.
questions.explanation: Compare results only under the same setup.

questions.prompt: What does MLPerf Training measure?
options: How long systems take to train models to a target quality
How fast systems serve trained models (latency)
How accurate models are on a fixed test set
How many parameters a model has
questions.answer: How long systems take to train models to a target quality
questions.explanation: It compares hardware and software systems.

questions.prompt: What is the name (abbreviation) of Stanford's holistic evaluation framework for language models?
questions.explanation: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models.

questions.prompt: Why do benchmark makers keep some test sets private or held out?
options: To reduce contamination and overfitting to the benchmark
To save storage and download costs
Because some questions have wrong answers
To keep scores comparable across years
questions.answer: To reduce contamination and overfitting to the benchmark
questions.explanation: Public test sets can leak into training data.

questions.prompt: What does the GSM8K benchmark test?
questions.explanation: It checks multi-step arithmetic reasoning.

questions.prompt: Tokens per second is a common performance metric for LLM inference.
questions.explanation: Along with time-to-first-token and latency.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Git and a GitHub repository?
options: Git is a version control tool that runs on your computer; a GitHub repository is a Git repository hosted online for sharing and collaboration
Git is a website; GitHub is the program you install
They are the same thing with two names
GitHub is required to use Git at all

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes how to turn an existing web app into a mobile app?
options: Make the site responsive, wrap it with a tool like Capacitor (or make it a PWA), add icons and native features, build it in Android Studio / Xcode, then publish to the app stores
Build it in Android Studio first, then make the site responsive, then add icons
Make it a PWA, then submit the website URL to the Apple App Store with no build step
Wrap it with Capacitor, then publish it to the stores without building it in Android Studio or Xcode
questions.answer: Make the site responsive, wrap it with a tool like Capacitor (or make it a PWA), add icons and native features, build it in Android Studio / Xcode, then publish to the app stores
questions.explanation: Common routes: a PWA (installable from the browser), a wrapper such as Capacitor or Cordova that puts the web app in a native shell, or a rewrite with React Native or Flutter. Store apps need signing, icons, privacy details and review.

questions.prompt: What does "freemium" mean when an AI tool is described as freemium?

The tool is completely free forever with no paid options
You must pay before you can try anything
The tool is open source and its code is free to change

questions.explanation: Free + premium: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini all have free tiers with paid plans for more usage and features. Open source is different: the code itself is free to use and modify.

questions.prompt: What is LangChain?
options: An open-source framework for building LLM apps and agents
A vector database for storing embeddings
A model gateway that routes to many LLM APIs
questions.answer: An open-source framework for building LLM apps and agents
questions.explanation: LangChain gives building blocks (models, prompts, tools, retrievers) and hundreds of integrations.

questions.prompt: Which LangChain product is used to trace, debug and evaluate LLM apps?
questions.explanation: LangSmith records every step of a run and lets you test prompts against datasets.

questions.prompt: How does LangGraph model an agent workflow?
options: As a graph of nodes and edges that share state and can loop
As one long prompt with all instructions
As a fixed straight-line chain only
As a list of independent tools with no shared state

questions.prompt: In LangGraph, what lets a run pause (for example for human approval) and resume later, even after a crash?

questions.prompt: LangSmith can trace and evaluate apps that are not built with LangChain.

questions.prompt: The LangChain library for building stateful, multi-step agents as graphs is called ___.

questions.prompt: Connect each part of the LangChain family to its role.
pairs: Building blocks and integrations for LLM apps
Joining steps with the | pipe operator

questions.prompt: What does a leaf node in a classification decision tree hold?
questions.explanation: Internal nodes test features; leaves give the prediction.

questions.prompt: Which measure is commonly used to choose splits in a classification decision tree?
questions.explanation: Gini impurity or entropy (information gain) measure how mixed the classes are after a split.

questions.prompt: A single very deep decision tree tends to overfit the training data.
questions.explanation: Limit depth, set a minimum leaf size or prune to reduce overfitting.

questions.prompt: How does a random forest differ from gradient boosting?
options: A forest trains trees independently and averages them; boosting adds trees one after another to fix earlier errors
A forest adds trees one by one; boosting trains them independently
A forest uses one deep tree; boosting uses many shallow ones
Boosting averages its trees; a forest keeps only the best tree
questions.answer: A forest trains trees independently and averages them; boosting adds trees one after another to fix earlier errors
questions.explanation: Bagging lowers variance; boosting lowers bias step by step.

questions.prompt: In decision theory, a rational agent picks the action with the highest expected ___.
questions.explanation: Expected utility = sum of probability x utility over the outcomes.

questions.prompt: Action A gives $100 with probability 0.5, otherwise $0. Action B gives $40 for sure. Which has the higher expected value?
questions.explanation: 0.5 x 100 = 50, which is more than 40. A risk-averse person may still choose B.

questions.prompt: Which list gives the parts of a Markov decision process (MDP)?
options: States, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor
Rows, columns and a hit policy
Features, labels and a loss function only
questions.answer: States, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor
questions.explanation: A policy maps states to actions to maximize expected discounted reward.

questions.prompt: In an MDP or reinforcement learning, what is the name for the rule that maps each state to an action?
questions.explanation: The goal of RL is to learn a good policy.

questions.prompt: What does a POMDP add to an MDP?
options: The agent cannot see the true state and must act on observations and a belief
questions.answer: The agent cannot see the true state and must act on observations and a belief
questions.explanation: Partially observable: the agent keeps a probability distribution (belief) over states.

questions.prompt: What is DMN?
options: Decision Model and Notation, an OMG standard for decision tables and decision diagrams
Data Model Notation, a database schema standard
Decision Making Network, a neural network type
Dynamic Model Navigator, a BPMN extension
questions.answer: Decision Model and Notation, an OMG standard for decision tables and decision diagrams
questions.explanation: DMN is supported by engines such as Camunda, Drools and IBM ODM.

questions.prompt: In a DMN decision table, what does the hit policy define?
options: What happens when more than one rule matches the inputs
The order in which tables are evaluated
How many rules the table can contain
questions.answer: What happens when more than one rule matches the inputs
questions.explanation: Examples: Unique, First, Priority, Any and Collect.

questions.prompt: For a fraud model, the best decision threshold is always 0.5.

The option with the highest weighted score
The option most stakeholders vote for

A full virtual machine with its own operating system
A compressed archive of source code

It is slower to start than a VM

Store for images, such as Docker Hub

questions.prompt: What is quantization of an AI model?

Removing layers to make the model smaller
Training a smaller model to copy a larger one
questions.answer: Storing weights with fewer bits to save memory and speed up inference
questions.explanation: For example FP16 → INT8 or 4-bit.

It removes layers from the model
It lets the model skip tokens it is confident about
questions.answer: Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, and smaller weights mean fewer bytes to read per token

QAT quantizes after training; PTQ trains with low precision
PTQ needs more training data than QAT

Easy 8-bit and 4-bit loading in Hugging Face

The settings people choose before training
questions.answer: The numbers the model learned during training that decide how inputs are turned into outputs

They change during each conversation with users
A search tries random values until one works

How much each weight affects the error

questions.prompt: What does CoWoS stand for?

To lower the price of consumer GPUs
To let the GPU use DDR5 system memory

The maximum clock speed of a GPU
The maximum number of GPUs in a server
The maximum power of a data centre

questions.prompt: During the 2023-2024 AI boom, CoWoS packaging capacity was one of the main bottlenecks limiting the supply of NVIDIA AI GPUs.

questions.explanation: All join several dies into one package for more bandwidth and more silicon.

An open GPU standard supported by all vendors

Always put the longer answer first

The share of all predictions that were right

The area under the ROC curve

questions.prompt: What is Ollama mainly used for?

questions.explanation: It can run models from many makers, such as Llama, Gemma, Qwen and Mistral.
options: Running open-weight AI models locally on your own computer
Training models from scratch in the cloud
Routing requests to many cloud model APIs

It is always faster than the cloud

questions.prompt: Why are models run with Ollama usually "quantized" (for example to 4-bit)?

To make them more accurate than the original

To make them follow instructions better

questions.prompt: What are Open WebUI and LibreChat?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a chat client like LibreChat and a model gateway like OpenRouter?

questions.explanation: They can be combined: a chat client can use a gateway as one of its providers.

They are exactly the same thing

questions.prompt: What is OpenClaw?
questions.answer: An open-source personal AI agent you run yourself, reached through chat apps
questions.explanation: It runs on your own computer or server and can act for you with tools.
options: An open-source personal AI agent you run yourself, reached through chat apps

questions.answer: A folder with a SKILL.md instruction file (and optional scripts) that adds an ability

A plugin that adds a new chat app

questions.explanation: It is what makes OpenClaw proactive rather than only replying.

Checks that the model API is online
Saves memory to disk every few minutes
Keeps the chat app connection alive

questions.prompt: OpenClaw keeps its memory as plain Markdown files on disk that you can read and edit.

questions.prompt: With OpenClaw you can talk to the same assistant from messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram.

The code was bought by Google
Users voted for a new name

options: A Reddit-style social network where AI agents post and humans mostly watch
A chat app built by Anthropic

questions.answer: Keep its control panel off the public internet, give it least-privilege accounts and require approval for sensitive actions

Install popular marketplace skills without reading them, since they are reviewed

questions.prompt: Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" for AI agents is the combination of which three things?
questions.answer: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally

questions.prompt: Skills from an agent marketplace are safe to install without checking, because the marketplace reviews every one.

questions.prompt: In generative AI, what is "confabulation"?
questions.answer: Confidently stated content that is false or not supported by facts
questions.explanation: It is the same problem usually called hallucination.
options: Confidently stated content that is false or not supported by facts
A model refusing to answer a safe question
Two models giving different answers to the same prompt
Output that is cut off by the token limit

questions.prompt: Which NIST document uses the term "confabulation" and lists it among the main risks of generative AI?
questions.explanation: Published in July 2024 as a companion to the NIST AI RMF.

questions.prompt: Where does the word "confabulation" originally come from?
questions.answer: Psychology and neurology, describing people who fill memory gaps with false details they believe
questions.explanation: For example in Korsakoff syndrome; there is no intent to deceive.
options: Psychology and neurology, describing people who fill memory gaps with false details they believe
Cybersecurity, describing a type of phishing attack
Linguistics, describing words borrowed from another language

questions.prompt: Confabulation means the AI model is deliberately lying to the user.
questions.explanation: Like the human condition it is named after, there is no intent to deceive: the model fills gaps with plausible text.

questions.prompt: Why do language models confabulate?
questions.answer: They predict likely next words rather than checked facts, and training often rewards guessing over saying "I don't know"
questions.explanation: OpenAI explained this link to training and evaluation in September 2025.
options: They predict likely next words rather than checked facts, and training often rewards guessing over saying "I don't know"
Their GPUs make random memory errors during inference
They are programmed to sound confident to win users
Their tokenizer drops words from the prompt

questions.prompt: Which kind of request is most likely to produce a confabulated answer?
questions.answer: Exact citations, quotes or numbers about a rare or very recent topic
questions.explanation: Models are least reliable on rare facts, recent events and precise references.
options: Exact citations, quotes or numbers about a rare or very recent topic
Rewriting a paragraph you pasted in more simply
Summarizing a document provided in the prompt

questions.prompt: A summary says a contract runs for 5 years when the provided contract says 3 years. Which type of confabulation is this?
questions.answer: Intrinsic: the output contradicts the source

options: Intrinsic: the output contradicts the source
Extrinsic: the output adds unverifiable details

questions.prompt: Which approach does most to reduce confabulation in a business assistant?
questions.answer: Ground answers in retrieved documents, require checkable citations and allow "I don't know"

options: Ground answers in retrieved documents, require checkable citations and allow "I don't know"
Set the temperature to 0 and trust the answer
Use a longer and more polite system prompt
Ask the model to sound more confident

questions.prompt: Setting the temperature to 0 stops a model from confabulating.

questions.prompt: Lawyers in Mata v. Avianca (2023) were sanctioned for citing court cases that ChatGPT had ___.
questions.explanation: A well-known real case of confabulation causing harm.

Using every programming language at once

questions.prompt: Which part of an app is the "frontend"?

By sharing the same database tables directly in the browser

questions.prompt: A developer who works on the frontend, the backend and the database is called a ___ developer.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between a Raspberry Pi and an Arduino?

Searching your documents at question time

Deleting a model's training data after release
Sending too many requests to slow a model down
Leaking user chats to the public

A prompt the model writes for itself
A list of banned words for the model
